Katalog Berita (Halaman 19/57)

#7744. Choosin' Texas I Can Tell

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

A few moments ago, the networks called the Texas Senate and Governor races for the Democratic candidates. Those outcomes will get a lot of attention. But of significant interest will be the downballot judicial races in Texas.

This year, four of the nine seats on the Texas Supreme Court were on the ballot. Unless something unexpected happens, all four will lose: Chief Justice Jimmy Blacklock, Justice James P. Sullivan, Justice Kyle Hawkins, and Justice Brett Busby. These are all brilliant judges. Three of them clerked on the United States Supreme Court. Chief Justice Blacklock has been a strong leader, following in the footsteps of Chief Justice Nathan Hecht. But the qualifications do not matter. Everything was on the party line. The Texas Supreme Court will now have five Republican members and four Democratic members. One might expect a number of 5-4 cases for controversial cases. Then again, the Chief Justice is now the administrator of the state court system, which entails some important responsibilities.

The Texas Court of Criminal Appeals (the court of last resort for criminal cases) had three seats on the ballot. Again, unless something happens, all three will lose. There will still be a six-member conservative majority. I don't see too much changing on that Court.

Recently, the Fifteenth Court of Appeals was created as a statewide constitutional court. Virtually all suits against the government are routed to that court. (Think of something like the D.C. Circuit.) All three members of that court were on the ballot. Unless something happens, all three will lose. The Court will now have 100% Democratic members. I would expect a lot mandamus suits to the Texas Supreme Court.

I haven't had time to go through the returns from the local courts, but it appears that most of the incumbent republican judges will lose office. This will be an even bigger bloodbath than 2018, when the Beto wave wiped out nearly all of the Republican judges in Houston, Austin, Dallas, and other large cities. So much judicial experience for non-controversial judges will go down the tube.

The Governor of Texas is fairly weak, as compared to other states, but he does have the power to appoint new members of the Texas Supreme Court and other courts when vacancies arise. Recently, the Texas legislature created a new Texas Business Court. This court was designed to compete with Delaware. Many of the current Texas business courts are not likely to be reappointed. This election will significantly affect businesses that chose to make Texas their headquarters. Speaking of which…

The Texas Attorney General Race will also likely go to the Democratic candidate. I would suspect that all of the conservative strategic litigation cases brought by Attorney General Paxton will be dismissed. Indeed, it is conceivable that the new Texas Attorney General would not defend the Texas Ten Commandments Law if cert is granted. (The BIO will be filed soon.) The Texas Attorney General will also not bring original jurisdiction actions before the Supreme Court of Texas. Going forward, all of the strategic forums in Texas will be severely underutilized. The only court where the Texas Attorney General might file cases will be in Austin. I should note that one seat on the Western District of Texas remained vacant for two years, and will likely remain vacant. But beyond the strategic litigation, the Texas Attorney General will now be able to investigate all of the corporations that moved to Texas. There are a lot of them.

What about judicial nominees? Despite my best efforts, Judge Southwick will get the last laugh. Todd Butler will almost certainly be confirmed. But the Fifth Circuit will likely be a lot quieter, given the lack of Texas Attorney General cases. I also hope this means that Judge Rudofsky will get a vote, as that Eighth Circuit seat would remain vacant for the foreseeable future. Indeed, the Eighth Circuit may be the only viable forum for a Republican AG to bring cases starting in 2026.

Going forward, Senators Cruz and Talarico will have to agree on blue slips for District Court nominees. Still, I suspect zero nominees will get a vote over the next two years unless there is some deal struck with the Senate Democrats.

What about Justices Alito and Thomas? They did what Justice Breyer could not--resist the pressure. I hope they live long and prosper.

Ultimately, I'm reminded of something I tell my students--we are never more than two years away from a midterm election. Despite threats about fascism and totalitarianism, the people are able to effect change.

NEXT: Court Orders Plaintiff to File Handwritten Opposition,

Josh Blackman is a constitutional law professor at the South Texas College of Law Houston and the President of the Harlan Institute. Follow him @JoshMBlackman.

#7743. Federal judge sides with Biden Labor Dept. on ESG fiduciary rule

A Texas Northern District Court judge said the rule is still valid under Loper Bright and does not violate the Employment Retirement Income Security Act of 1974.

The Labor Department rule in question, “Prudence and Loyalty in Selecting Plan Investments and Exercising Shareholder Rights,” was finalized in 2022 and has been in effect since January 2023. The rule was designed to overturn guidance the agency issued in 2020 under the first Trump administration that forbade fiduciaries from utilizing “non-pecuniary” factors in investment decisions.

The 2022 rule was designed to overturn a “chilling effect” that the Biden administration’s Labor Department said was witnessed under the 2020 rule. The guidance revised the agency’s tiebreaker standard to allow for consideration of collateral benefits like ESG in the event that two or more investments would equally serve the plan’s best interests but it would be imprudent to invest in both or all options.

The DOL rule has been repeatedly challenged by a coalition of 26 Republican-led states, who argued it runs afoul of ERISA and exceeded the agency’s statutory authority. However, Kacsmaryk disagreed in his Feb. 14 ruling and said such a reading of the law “embodies the wooden textualism that courts should endeavor to avoid.”

“Under the rule, a fiduciary faced with choosing between investment options — that all equally serve the beneficiaries' financial interests — does not advance the interests of nonbeneficiaries nor act for a purpose other than their financial benefit when he chooses based on collateral factors,” the judge ruled. “Plaintiffs' interpretation of ERISA would demand arbitrary randomness to choose between such investment options.”

The Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo case — which determined the fate of the Chevron doctrine — was decided in the time between Kacsmaryk’s initial dismissal of the case and when the plaintiffs and the Biden administration’s Labor Department argued before the U.S. Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals. The Supreme Court’s decision in June 2024 overturned the Chevron doctrine, which previously directed courts to give agencies deference in their interpretations of ambiguous law statutes.

While the parties had opposing views on how Chevron’s demise affected the case at hand, the Fifth Circuit refused to rule on the case, but vacated the initial dismissal and asked Kacsmaryk whether the rule can be squared with ERISA or the Administrative Procedure Act in light of Loper Bright.

Kacsmaryk said Loper Bright “did not disturb how courts evaluate a rule under the APA's arbitrary and capricious standard,” in his ruling Friday. He said the overturn of the Chevron doctrine should change how courts should interpret statutes, but not how they review the reasonableness of agency decisions.

The judge said that the tiebreaker standard in the 2022 rule does not violate ERISA’s duty of loyalty nor its requirement that fiduciaries act “solely” and for the “exclusive” benefit of the plan’s financial interests. Kacsmaryk said ERISA defines “whose interest the fiduciary must protect” and what their purpose is, but “says nothing of what they may consider.”

“Just as a driver, duty-bound to choose the fastest route to his destination, may choose the most scenic of two routes that each bring him to his destination at the same time, so too can a fiduciary choose a preferable investment option between two that will equally satisfy his duty of loyalty,” the judge wrote.

The coalition of Republican-led states were also joined in their lawsuit by public oilfield services company Liberty Energy, where Energy Secretary Chris Wright served as CEO at the time. The plaintiffs have previously signaled a willingness to fight the case all the way to the Supreme Court, but first it will return to the Fifth Circuit panel that initially heard the arguments.

However, it remains to be seen how the Trump administration’s Labor Department will handle the case. Experts have previously expressed concerns about the DOL’s rule being one of the Biden administration’s ESG-related regulations likely to be put on the chopping block under Trump.

#7742. Racial comments to attorney sparked investigation of federal judge

U.S. District Judge Ada Brown of the Northern District of Texas is accused of making racial comments to an attorney. (Photo from Facebook/Judge Ada Brown for SCOTUS)

A lawyer who filed a misconduct complaint against a federal judge in Dallas did so after a hearing during which she repeatedly directed racial insults at him, Bloomberg Law reports.

Documents show that attorney Ezra Young, who represented a Black woman professor suing over a tenure denial, filed the complaint following the April hearing in Dallas. His complaint and the response from U.S. District Judge Ada Brown of the Northern District of Texas were among the documents that Brown circulated in an Oct. 17 email to lawyers, judges and members of the media, Bloomberg Law reports.

Throughout the hearing, Brown, a Black woman with Native American ancestry, accused Young of mistreating Black attorneys, took “judicial notice” of her own background in making findings against Young, and repeatedly referred to Young, who is Latino, as being white.

“I think what’s happening here, quite candidly, is you are very intimidated for some reason, Mr. Young, with Black excellence, in light of your white mediocrity. Yeah. Right?,” Brown said, according to the transcript. “You should write that down. I mean, you—I’m—you look like a white man, right?”

“I’m not white, your honor,” Young replied, adding that he’s Latino.

Young filed the complaint, saying he thought that the judge may be suffering from a mental health condition. A judicial investigation resulted in her temporarily losing her docket earlier this month. A special judicial committee has ordered Brown to undergo a psychiatric examination as part of that investigation.

#7741. Federal Judge Alvin Hellerstein of New York dies at 92

In this courtroom sketch, U.S. District Judge Alvin Hellerstein of the Southern District of New York presides during a pretrial hearing in a drug trafficking case for former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, on July 22, 2026, in New York. (Photo by Jane Rosenberg via the Associated Press)

U.S. District Judge Alvin Hellerstein of the Southern District of New York died Wednesday at age 92.

Hellerstein was known for presiding over the federal narcoterrorism conspiracy case against ousted Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, according to a story from Law.com. He also oversaw more than 14,000 lawsuits that were filed by victims of the Sept. 11 terror attacks.

On a personal level, the judge is being remembered for his empathy and morality, which was informed by his Jewish faith.

“He didn’t shy away from pushing the boundaries of the law if he thought they would be unjust otherwise,” Evan Farber, a partner at Loeb & Loeb who once clerked for Hellerstein, told Law.com.

Hellerstein graduated from Columbia Law School in 1956, and he became a clerk for U.S. District Judge Edmund Palmieri of the Southern District of New York, Law.com reports. He was a military lawyer with the U.S. Army and a partner and a litigator at Stroock & Stroock & Lavan before being nominated to the federal bench by then-President Bill Clinton. He was confirmed unanimously in 1998.

He took senior status in 2011, but he never slowed down, Law.com reports.

#7740. In broad sweep, EEOC moves to abandon its pending gender identity bias lawsuits

In its motions to dismiss, the agency pointed to President Donald Trump’s executive order on “gender ideology extremism” and guidance from the Office of Personnel Management.

The U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission has requested dismissal of nearly every lawsuit it filed in the previous year alleging discrimination against a transgender worker or workers, less than one month after Acting Chair Andrea Lucas announced the agency would focus on “rolling back the Biden administration’s gender identity agenda.”

According to court filings viewed by HR Dive, EEOC last week filed motions to dismiss at least six pending lawsuits. These include cases against a Holiday Inn Express owner; the owner of a Home2 Suites by Hilton hotel in Alabama; an Illinois hog farm; a pizzeria located in Chicago O’Hare International Airport; a Wendy’s operator based in southern Illinois; and a Lush location based in California’s Bay Area.

The complaints included a range of charges, including employers’ tolerance of deadnaming, misgendering, “outing,” and harassing and invasive comments from co-workers. Multiple lawsuits alleged retaliation, with workers reporting they had been fired after coming to their supervisors with complaints about the conduct.

EEOC filed the lawsuits under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, which the U.S. Supreme Court determined to include employment discrimination on the basis of gender identity and sexual orientation in the landmark 2020 Bostock v. Clayton County, Ga. case.

In its motions to dismiss, the majority of which were filed Friday and used largely the same language, the agency pointed to President Donald Trump’s executive order on “gender ideology extremism” and to guidance from the Office of Personnel Management requiring all federal employees to comply with the order.

“The EEOC’s continued litigation of the claim in this action may be inconsistent with the Order and the OPM Guidance,” the agency stated in each motion.

“This dereliction of EEOC’s duty under its legal mandate requires immediate judicial intervention,” Equal Rights Advocates, a legal group that advocates for “gender justice in workplaces,” said in a statement Tuesday on the move. “Transgender and gender non-conforming employees deserve the full protection of our civil rights laws, as established by Congress and the Supreme Court, not selective enforcement based on political whims and hastily issued executive orders.”

EEOC told HR Dive it would not comment on litigation.

#7738. Former U.S. Government Contractor Pleads Guilty to Spying for Ethiopia

An official website of the United States government

Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( Lock Locked padlock ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

Abraham Teklu Lemma, 53, of Maryland, a former information technology contractor at the National Reconnaissance Office, the U.S. Department of State, and the U.S. Department of Justice pleaded guilty today to conspiring to commit espionage on behalf of the government of the Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia.

Lemma pleaded guilty to conspiracy to transmit national defense information to a foreign government and has agreed to be incarcerated for a period of between 120 and 262 months.

“Lemma betrayed the United States to an extraordinary degree,” said Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg. “He exploited his IT administrator access to remove classified national defense information, including Top Secret information, from a secure facility and transmitted it to Ethiopian government officials hoping they would use it to target and kill paramilitary fighters in a regional conflict. Clearance holders pledge undivided loyalty to the United States and bear a legal and moral responsibility to protect classified information. Those who betray this trust will be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law.”

“For more than two years, Lemma exploited a position of trust to provide highly classified U.S. government information to a foreign government,” said U.S. Attorney Jeanine Ferris Pirro for the District of Columbia. “In doing so, he betrayed his oath, his colleagues, and his country, while jeopardizing our national security. His guilty plea sends a clear message: those who compromise America’s most sensitive secrets will be investigated, prosecuted, and held accountable.”

“Despite swearing an oath to defend the Constitution of the United States, Abraham Lemma betrayed our country by committing espionage on behalf of the Ethiopian government,” said Assistant Director Roman Rozhavsky of the FBI’s Counterintelligence and Espionage Division. “By his own admission, Lemma provided classified national defense information to Ethiopian officials, who then used it in military operations during an ongoing conflict. This guilty plea should serve notice that the FBI and our partners will work tirelessly to stop foreign intelligence services, and anyone who decides to work with them, against the interests of the United States.”

“Today’s guilty plea makes clear that any attempt to betray the United States, violate the trust of the American people, and compromise our national security will not be tolerated,” said Assistant Director in Charge Darren B. Cox of the FBI Washington Field Office. “Lemma abused his position of trust and access to some of our nation’s most highly classified information, conspiring with foreign government officials to unlawfully disclose materials protected to the highest level. In doing so, he not only endangered our national security but also betrayed the trust placed in him by the American people.”

According to court documents, Lemma held a Top Secret U.S. security clearance. From 2021 until his arrest in August 2023, Lemma conspired with senior Ethiopian government officials to collect and transmit dozens of highly classified documents, notes, materials, and photographs, classified up to the Top Secret/Sensitive Compartmented Information (TS/SCI) level, to Ethiopian government officials. Material identified as “Top Secret” means that unauthorized disclosure of the material is reasonably to cause “exceptionally grave damage to the national security” of the United States.

Much of the highly classified information Lemma shared with the Ethiopian government concerned an armed conflict in Ethiopia. Lemma’s conspirators included senior officials within political, military, and intelligence branches of the Ethiopian government.

During his espionage activities, Lemma took numerous steps to conceal his conduct. and surreptitiously removed classified documents and information from U.S. government holdings.

Specifically, Lemma wrote notes by hand with classified information and then hand-carried those notes out of secure U.S. government facilities. Additionally, as an IT administrator, Lemma removed electronic versions of classified information from classified U.S. government repositories and then removed the same classified information from secure U.S. government facilities where he worked.

On some occasions, Lemma encouraged his Ethiopian government conspirators to take direct action against paramilitary groups who were fighting the government of Ethiopia. For example, on Dec. 18, 2021, Lemma told one conspirator, “We have to finish these people once and for all, otherwise there will never be peace in Ethiopia.” Later that day, Lemma shared additional information with his conspirator and wrote, “Please send Dro[nes].”

According to the plea agreement, Lemma agreed to plead guilty to conspiracy to transmit national defense information to a foreign government. If accepted by the court, Lemma has agreed to be incarcerated for a period of between 120 and 262 months. Sentencing is set for April 14, 2027.

The investigation was conducted by the FBI Washington Field Office.

The matter is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorneys Tejpal Chawla and Adam P. Barry for the District of Columbia, and Trial Attorney Kathryn DeMarco of the Department of Justice’s National Security Division.

#7734. Ohio Supreme Court suspends law license of attorney convicted of voting multiple times

The Ohio Supreme Court on Monday suspended the law license of a man convicted of illegally voting in Ohio and Florida in 2020 and 2022. (Image from Shutterstock)

The Ohio Supreme Court on Monday suspended the law license of a man convicted of illegally voting in both Ohio and Florida in 2020 and 2022.

James Saunders, a former attorney for the IRS, was convicted of two felony counts of illegal voting after casting ballots in both Cuyahoga County, Ohio, and Broward County, Florida, during the 2020 and 2022 general elections. His last known business address is in Washington, D.C., according to the state supreme court in its Oct. 26 order.

The state supreme court imposed the suspension after Saunders failed to answer a disciplinary complaint filed by the Cleveland Metropolitan Bar Association, according to a story by Cleveland.com.

Saunders had previously been disbarred in Florida. His suspension in Ohio is indefinite, the Ohio Supreme Court said, and he “will not be reinstated to the practice of law in Ohio until such time as respondent is reinstated to the practice of law in the state of Florida.”

#7729. Trump order tightens White House grip on Fed, SEC

Under the order, independent agencies must submit for review “significant” regulations to a unit within the Office of Management and Budget, and OMB Director Russ Vought has power over agency budgets.

Agencies such as the Securities and Exchange Commission, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission and the Federal Trade Commission – which Congress established as independent from the White House – would also be affected by the order.

The carve-out for the Fed on monetary policy “seems directed toward preventing a negative market reaction to the order,” said Jeff Naimon, a Washington, D.C.-based partner at law firm Orrick.

The agencies also have to employ a White House liaison, and consult regularly on policy and priorities with the OMB, the White House Domestic Policy Council and the White House National Economic Council, according to the order.  The OMB will “adjust so-called independent agencies’ apportionments to ensure tax dollars are spent wisely,” according to a fact sheet that accompanied the executive order.

“These regulatory agencies currently exercise substantial executive authority without sufficient accountability to the President, and through him, to the American people,” the order said. “Moreover, these regulatory agencies have been permitted to promulgate significant regulations without review by the President.”

The move to expand Trump’s authority is the latest by an administration that’s sought to concentrate power under the executive branch. It also reflects the influence of Vought, one of the architects of conservative blueprint Project 2025, and broadens his supervisory powers. In addition to leading OMB, Vought also is acting director of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau.

“For the Federal Government to be truly accountable to the American people, officials who wield vast executive power must be supervised and controlled by the people’s elected President,” the order continued.

Naimon noted there was strong coordination between independent agencies and the White House during Trump’s prior administration, but the executive order would now require that coordination.

Legal challenges to the order are “almost certain,” Kathryn Judge, a Columbia University professor of law, said in an email.

The outcome of any litigation is less clear, however, since the judiciary has embraced a more unitary view of the executive branch and a more expansive view of executive authority, she added.

The order “represents the largest single assertion over executive power over the administrative state that I can recall, not only in my lifetime but through history,” Peter Conti-Brown, a professor of financial regulation at the University of Pennsylvania’s Wharton School, said in an email. “Some aspects of this control represent departures from long-standing norms. Others are in apparent contravention of statute and will be challenged legally.”

“How much of the modern independent regulatory system survives the Trump Administration’s efforts at consolidation is anyone’s guess,” Conti-Brown said, noting that the Supreme Court has repeatedly expressed skepticism of independent agencies. SCOTUS did, however, uphold the funding structure of the CFPB.

Banks may welcome the development in the near term, since the Trump administration is widely expected to usher in an era of reduced regulatory burden. But “those shifts would be far less enduring than if implemented in other ways,” Judge said.

“Longer term, the result may be a whipsaw in regulatory and supervisory expectations,” she said. “That will make it harder for banks to make operational and other decisions that are core to their business.”

#7725. Man Pleads Guilty to Federal Hate Crimes in Deadly Attack on Boulder, Colorado, Gathering

An official website of the United States government

Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( Lock Locked padlock ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

Mohamed Sabry Soliman, 46, of Colorado Springs, Colorado, pleaded guilty in federal court today to 12 hate crimes charges for using Molotov cocktails to attack members of the group Run for Their Lives and others.

As part of the plea agreement, Soliman admitted that on June 1, 2025, he lit and threw two Molotov cocktails into a gathering of the Boulder chapter of Run for Their Lives, a group that organized walks throughout the United States to raise awareness for hostages still held after the October 7, 2023, terrorist attacks in Israel. Soliman further admitted that he targeted the group because of the victims’ actual or perceived Israeli national origin and Jewish religion. The attack killed one person and caused permanent and life-threatening injuries to several others.

“No one should be subjected to violence because of their religion or national origin,” said Assistant Attorney General Harmeet K. Dhillon of the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division. “With this plea, we hope to deliver a measure of justice to the victims and their families. The Civil Rights Division remains committed to vigorously prosecuting the perpetrators of bias-motivated violence.”

“By his own admissions, Mohamed Soliman’s hateful attack on our neighbors in Boulder was antisemitic,” said U.S. Attorney for the District of Colorado Peter McNeilly. “All Americans should feel free to pursue their faith and way of life without fear that doing so will put their personal safety at risk. Antisemitism erodes the common ties that bind our great nation together and there is no place for it in America. We are grateful for the trust and support of the victims and the Boulder community as we prosecuted this case.”

“This individual conducted a despicable attack on people he believed to be Jewish or who support Israel, and with today’s plea he is admitting his guilt,” said Assistant Director Jarod Brown of the FBI’s Counterterrorism Division. “The FBI is steadfast in our commitment to protect our communities and uphold the Constitution.  We will continue to work with our Justice Department partners to ensure those who harm others or attempt to intimidate those expressing their personal views are held accountable.”

“The chaos inflicted by this defendant spread its seeds far beyond Pearl Street, Boulder, and Colorado,” said Special Agent in Charge Amanda Koldjeski of the FBI Denver Field Office. “FBI Denver is proud of the role we played in this case alongside our partners in Boulder: We do not tolerate acts of hate and terror against our neighbors. We will continue to work to keep our community safe and seek justice for victims.”

For nine of his hate crimes charges, Soliman faces a maximum penalty of life in prison, five years of supervised release, and a fine of up to $250,000. For the three other hate crimes charges, Soliman faces a maximum penalty of 50 years in prison to run consecutive to any other prison term, three years of supervised release, and a fine of up to $250,000. A federal district court judge will determine any sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors. A sentencing hearing is scheduled for Jan. 7, 2027.

The FBI Denver Field Office and the Boulder Police Department investigated the case.

Assistant U.S. Attorneys Melissa Basche and Daniel Pastor for the District of Colorado and Trial Attorneys Sarah Howard and Khalil Quinan of the Civil Rights Division’s Criminal Section are prosecuting the case.

Artificial intelligence developer Anthropic announced Wednesday the release of Claude for Legal artifacts, with plans to provide users with 12 practice group-specific plug-ins and connectors to over 60 other legal platforms. (Image from Shutterstock)

Artificial intelligence developer Anthropic announced Wednesday the release of Claude for Legal artifacts, with plans to provide users with 12 practice group-specific plug-ins and connectors to over 60 other legal platforms.

Claude for Legal’s expansion encompasses reusable digital products, or artifacts, featuring tools, dashboards and workflows. The release of about 18 artifacts for commercial legal work will be tailored for intake, tabular review, regulatory tracking, jurisdiction surveys and citation confirmation. Users will have the option of customizing the artifacts and designing their own, according to coverage by Law.com.

Anthropic’s artifacts release continues a trend in Big Tech that includes Microsoft, Legora and OpenAI, which also launched legal-specific tools. Anthropic is also unveiling artifacts designed by partner organizations Goodwin Procter, Foley & Lardner, Harvey and PricewaterhouseCoopers. In addition, the company will launch a program for law schools and justice-oriented organizations that provides them with Claude seat licenses and application programming interface.

“We heard from legal users that they wanted something that was a little bit easier to use and adapt, rather than this blank screen that the Claude chat experience is,” said Robert Mahari, the head of Claude for Legal. “You can now take this, and it’s pretty close to ready to use.”

James Thomas Ashbacher, 37, of Spring Lake, North Carolina, a former U.S. government contractor, was arrested by the FBI on Tuesday for allegedly leaking national defense information by posting the information on a popular social media site, unlawfully retaining other national defense information at his residence, and stealing night vision goggles from the U.S. Army’s Special Operations Command.

Ashbacher was charged by an indictment unsealed Tuesday with unlawfully transmitting and retaining national defense information and with theft of government property.

According to the indictment, beginning in or about 2021, the defendant worked as an employee of a private company that provided security and emergency management services at the U.S. Army Special Operations Command facility in Fort Bragg, North Carolina. To perform the required functions of his employment, Ashbacher held a Top Secret security clearance with Sensitive Compartmented Information (SCI) access.

As further detailed in the indictment, Ashbacher photographed and removed without authorization videos and photographs containing images of classified military operations and transmitted the materials to a social media site. The classified materials were later re-posted by other users to a second social media site. Ashbacher asked a social media user in a private message to remove some materials and further stated that he was “trying to do some damage control.” A search of Ashbacher’s residence also revealed a classified award write-up that contained additional national defense information, along with a night vision goggle system specific to a military unit within Army Special Operations Command that had been reported missing.

The FBI Charlotte Field Office is investigating the case with substantial assistance from the U.S. Department of the Army’s Criminal Investigative Division.

Trial Attorney Leslie Esbrook of the National Security Division’s Counterintelligence and Export Control Section and Assistant U.S. Attorney Logan Liles for the Eastern District of North Carolina are prosecuting the case.

An indictment is merely an allegation. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.

#7718. Former U.S. Government Contractor Pleads Guilty to Spying for Ethiopia

An official website of the United States government

Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( Lock Locked padlock ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

Abraham Teklu Lemma, 53, of Maryland, a former information technology contractor at the National Reconnaissance Office, the U.S. Department of State, and the U.S. Department of Justice pleaded guilty today to conspiring to commit espionage on behalf of the government of the Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia.

Lemma pleaded guilty to conspiracy to transmit national defense information to a foreign government and has agreed to be incarcerated for a period of between 120 and 262 months.

“Lemma betrayed the United States to an extraordinary degree,” said Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg. “He exploited his IT administrator access to remove classified national defense information, including Top Secret information, from a secure facility and transmitted it to Ethiopian government officials hoping they would use it to target and kill paramilitary fighters in a regional conflict. Clearance holders pledge undivided loyalty to the United States and bear a legal and moral responsibility to protect classified information. Those who betray this trust will be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law.”

“For more than two years, Lemma exploited a position of trust to provide highly classified U.S. government information to a foreign government,” said U.S. Attorney Jeanine Ferris Pirro for the District of Columbia. “In doing so, he betrayed his oath, his colleagues, and his country, while jeopardizing our national security. His guilty plea sends a clear message: those who compromise America’s most sensitive secrets will be investigated, prosecuted, and held accountable.”

“Despite swearing an oath to defend the Constitution of the United States, Abraham Lemma betrayed our country by committing espionage on behalf of the Ethiopian government,” said Assistant Director Roman Rozhavsky of the FBI’s Counterintelligence and Espionage Division. “By his own admission, Lemma provided classified national defense information to Ethiopian officials, who then used it in military operations during an ongoing conflict. This guilty plea should serve notice that the FBI and our partners will work tirelessly to stop foreign intelligence services, and anyone who decides to work with them, against the interests of the United States.”

“Today’s guilty plea makes clear that any attempt to betray the United States, violate the trust of the American people, and compromise our national security will not be tolerated,” said Assistant Director in Charge Darren B. Cox of the FBI Washington Field Office. “Lemma abused his position of trust and access to some of our nation’s most highly classified information, conspiring with foreign government officials to unlawfully disclose materials protected to the highest level. In doing so, he not only endangered our national security but also betrayed the trust placed in him by the American people.”

According to court documents, Lemma held a Top Secret U.S. security clearance. From 2021 until his arrest in August 2023, Lemma conspired with senior Ethiopian government officials to collect and transmit dozens of highly classified documents, notes, materials, and photographs, classified up to the Top Secret/Sensitive Compartmented Information (TS/SCI) level, to Ethiopian government officials. Material identified as “Top Secret” means that unauthorized disclosure of the material is reasonably to cause “exceptionally grave damage to the national security” of the United States.

Much of the highly classified information Lemma shared with the Ethiopian government concerned an armed conflict in Ethiopia. Lemma’s conspirators included senior officials within political, military, and intelligence branches of the Ethiopian government.

During his espionage activities, Lemma took numerous steps to conceal his conduct. and surreptitiously removed classified documents and information from U.S. government holdings.

Specifically, Lemma wrote notes by hand with classified information and then hand-carried those notes out of secure U.S. government facilities. Additionally, as an IT administrator, Lemma removed electronic versions of classified information from classified U.S. government repositories and then removed the same classified information from secure U.S. government facilities where he worked.

On some occasions, Lemma encouraged his Ethiopian government conspirators to take direct action against paramilitary groups who were fighting the government of Ethiopia. For example, on Dec. 18, 2021, Lemma told one conspirator, “We have to finish these people once and for all, otherwise there will never be peace in Ethiopia.” Later that day, Lemma shared additional information with his conspirator and wrote, “Please send Dro[nes].”

According to the plea agreement, Lemma agreed to plead guilty to conspiracy to transmit national defense information to a foreign government. If accepted by the court, Lemma has agreed to be incarcerated for a period of between 120 and 262 months. Sentencing is set for April 14, 2027.

The investigation was conducted by the FBI Washington Field Office.

The matter is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorneys Tejpal Chawla and Adam P. Barry for the District of Columbia, and Trial Attorney Kathryn DeMarco of the Department of Justice’s National Security Division.

Waukesha County Presiding Judge Michael P. Maxwell, who consulted first with the chief judge and the clerk of court, issued the order after the Brewers captured their first-ever World Series title in franchise history, defeating the Tampa Bay Rays on Wednesday, Fox6 News Milwaukee reports.

“While every day our courts deal with very serious issues, like child custody disputes and holding criminals accountable, the last few weeks have seen Brewer fever in many off-the-record conversations between lawyers, parties and court staff,” Maxwell wrote in a statement.

#7715. Oklahoma Man Charged in Connection with Sending Threatening Letters Containing Non-Toxic White Powder to Election and Government Officials Across the Country

An official website of the United States government

Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( Lock Locked padlock ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

Robin Patrick Martin, 67, of Oklahoma City, has been charged with conveying false or misleading information and hoaxes and mailing threatening communications in connection with threatening letters mailed to state election officials, members of Congress, the FBI and others.

“As alleged, Martin mailed letters containing white powder to hundreds of state and federal officials, a calculated attempt to terrorize public servants,” said Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg. “These officials were left to open those letters not knowing if the powder inside could sicken or even kill them, and that was the evident intent. Intimidation like this has no place in a Nation governed by the rule of law, and the National Security Division will investigate and prosecute these cases to the fullest extent appropriate.”

“Threatening election officials and attempting to intimidate public servants is a serious federal offense and will not be tolerated,” said U.S. Attorney Robert J. Troester for the Western District of Oklahoma. “Working alongside our federal law enforcement partners, we are committed to investigating these threats and holding accountable those who seek to spread fear and intimidation in our communities.”

“Early Monday morning, the FBI conducted an operation and arrested Robin Patrick Martin – the subject who allegedly sent hundreds of letters containing suspicious white powder substances to public officials around the country both before the 2024 and 2026 election,” said FBI Director Kash Patel. “The letters went to well over 100 locations including multiple state secretary offices, election offices, and more. The alleged subject had avoided authorities until now – as the Biden administration failed to catch him – but this FBI got it done. I want to thank our Oklahoma City Field Office and the FBI Criminal Division, as well as our USPIS, Capitol Police, and OKC PD partners who responded to the threat quickly and did outstanding work executing in this case. Every American citizen deserves a free and fair election – and anyone who attempts to undermine that process by breaking our laws and threatening public officials will be brought to justice.”

“The mailing of letters containing an unknown powdery substance across the country created unnecessary fear, diverted resources, and attempted to disrupt our nation’s democratic process,” said Special Agent in Charge Doug Goodwater of the FBI Oklahoma City Field Office. “No one should have to wonder whether a letter in the mail poses a danger, and the arrest of Robin Martin demonstrates that those who seek to spread panic and intimidation cannot expect to remain anonymous. I would like to express my gratitude to the dedicated team at FBI Oklahoma City and our partners at the US Attorney’s Offices, USPIS, USPS, U.S. Capitol Police, FBI Laboratory Division, and Oklahoma City Department for all their work in this matter.”

“The Postal Inspection Service has a long, proud, and successful history of ensuring the sanctity of election mail, safeguarding the integrity of elections, and protecting election officials from threatening and dangerous mail,” said Chief Postal Inspector Gary Barksdale of the U.S. Postal Inspection Service (USPIS). “Utilizing our expertise in the Postal Service and mail flow, postal inspectors and our partners identified related mailings and recovered the majority of these mailings before they reached their intended recipients, keeping Postal Service customers — the American public — safe. This arrest reflects the perseverance of the Postal Inspection Service, FBI, U.S. Capitol Police, and all of our law enforcement partners to keep criminals from interfering with two trusted traditions — the election process, and the U.S. Mail.”

“Our team has been working around the clock with our law enforcement partners to put this defendant behind bars,” said U.S. Capitol Police Chief Michael Sullivan. “We will not tolerate anyone who attempts to use fear as a weapon.”

According to public records, on Oct. 13, 2026, the Oklahoma State Election Board notified the FBI that it had received a threatening letter containing white powder. The FBI and USPIS had been investigating threatening letters containing white powder sent to multiple state election officials — including the Oklahoma State Election Board — since 2024. The FBI and USPIS determined that this letter was part of hundreds of threatening letters, many of which had white powder, that had been sent across the country to state election boards, members of Congress, election pollsters, media organizations, and others. The white powder was later determined to be non-hazardous.

Today, Martin appeared before U.S. Magistrate Judge Shon Erwin for his initial appearance in Oklahoma City.

This case is part of the nationwide National Security Presidential Memorandum 7 initiative, which is a White House-directed, interagency effort to integrate federal, state, and local partners in protecting First Amendment rights while targeting individuals and organizations engaged in political violence.

This case is being investigated by the FBI, USPIS, United States Capitol Police, Oklahoma City Police Department, and Texas Department of Public Safety, including the Texas Rangers, with valuable assistance from the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Oklahoma.

The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Western District of Oklahoma is prosecuting the case with assistance from the National Security Division’s Counterterrorism Section.

A complaint is merely an allegation. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.

#7711. Pactiv Evergreen settles for $6.25M over 2023 North Carolina mill closure

The restitution amount is more than half of what Pactiv Evergreen received from the state in economic development grants for the site.

The paper mill in Canton had been in operation for more than 100 years prior to then-owner Pactiv shutting it down in 2023, according to the state of North Carolina. Blue Ridge Paper Products operated the facility since 1999, and in 2007 that company became Evergreen Packaging through a merger. Pactiv Evergreen formed in 2020 through the combination of Evergreen Packaging and Pactiv, both of which were previously acquired by Reynolds Group Holdings.

At the time of the Canton mill’s closure, many people expressed surprise at Pactiv Evergreen’s decision. The company made the announcement in March 2023 along with other closure and restructuring disclosures, and CEO Mike King noted a “challenging market environment” for Pactiv’s beverage merchandising business. North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper said in a statement last week that the Canton closure came as a “gut punch" to the local and state economies.

Upon introducing the lawsuit in May 2024, then-Attorney General Josh Stein noted that taxpayers “invested in Pactiv Evergreen to bolster our state’s economy,” but Pactiv didn’t hold up its end of the bargain. He said at the time that his office had tried working with Pactiv for a year to address the company’s obligations, but it had “become clear that legal action was necessary to hold Pactiv accountable.” The initial lawsuit sought repayment of the full $12 million in economic incentives that Pactiv had received.

The settlement should not be viewed as an admission to wrongdoing, according to the North Carolina Department of Justice.

“Pactiv broke its promise to the state and the people of Canton, and today’s settlement holds it accountable for violating its agreement,” Attorney General Jeff Jackson, who was elected in November and took office last month, said of the new settlement. “This settlement will allow the people of Canton and Haywood County to immediately put millions back into rebuilding their economy after the mill’s closure, and it will shield them from future litigation from Pactiv.”

The candidates for state attorney general repeatedly brought up the mill issues on the campaign trail prior to November’s election. Both candidates expressed a desire to hold Pactiv accountable.

Pactiv had filed a motion to dismiss the complaint in July 2024. But a judge denied that motion in October, allowing the lawsuit to proceed.

“We are pleased to have resolved with the State of North Carolina all outstanding matters relating to the closure and sale of our former Canton mill site. We thank our employees for their contributions to our company and wish the Canton community well in this next chapter for the Town,” said Pactiv Evergreen Tuesday in an emailed statement.

This wasn’t Pactiv’s first legal battle over the Canton site.

In autumn 2023, the company reached a settlement worth more than $2 million with the U.S. EPA over Clean Air Act violations at Canton. Earlier that year, the North Carolina Department of Environmental Quality said the site violated water quality requirements; the company denied the allegations. In 2021 and 2022, the mill faced state air quality violations.

Novolex is in the process of acquiring Pactiv Evergreen for $6.7 billion. The deal, which would take Pactiv private, is expected to close during the first half of this year.

#7708. Law firms face increasing AI-fueled cyberattacks, new report says

Researchers are warning that cyberattacks using agentic artificial intelligence on law firms and other groups in the legal profession are on the rise. (Image from Shutterstock)

Researchers are warning that cyberattacks using agentic artificial intelligence on law firms and other groups in the legal profession are on the rise.

These attacks have doubled since 2023, according to cybersecurity company CrowdStrike’s 2026 Legal Threat Landscape Report, which was released Wednesday.

The report shows that between August 2025 and August 2026, cyber adversaries named 455 legal entities as hacking targets, an increase of 39% from the prior year.

While CrowdStrike did not name specific firms or other legal groups as the victims of attacks, Reuters has reported that Quinn Emanuel Urquhart & Sullivan, Wilmer Cutler Pickering Hale and Dorr and Seyfarth Shaw are among those that have experienced cyber breaches in recent months.

“What we’re seeing across the broader threat landscape, more and more threat actors are using agentic technology ⁠to democratize hacking,” said Adam Meyers, CrowdStrike’s senior vice president for counter adversary operations. “It’s going to get a lot worse before it gets better.”

#7703. What businesses should know about consent rules when calling consumers

Rules around obtaining consumer consent before calling or texting are in a state of legal and regulatory uncertainty – and companies should remain cautious.

Senosiain is an associate and Rollins is a shareholder at Gunster. Views are the authors’ own.

The Telephone Consumer Protection Act governs calls and text messages sent by businesses to consumers. One such rule is that businesses must obtain express written consent prior to sending text messages to consumers, if they are using an automated telephone dialing system or making calls using an artificial or pre-recorded voice, including the use of AI bots.

The TCPA also provides that businesses may not call or text consumers on the federal Do Not Call List unless prior express consent is given. Even basic telemarketing calls and text messages require prior express consent. Violation of the statute can trigger liability for up to $1,500 per call or text message sent.

Additionally, many states have their own version of the TCPA, deemed “mini-TCPAs,” that require compliance for all businesses who make calls to consumer-residents in that state, regardless of where the business is domiciled.

Many companies use lead generators which gather consumer consents for multiple businesses and then provide the companies with consent and contact information for those potential consumers. Lead generators who obtain proper written consent can be a very useful tool for companies. This was generally permissible under the TCPA.

However, in 2023, the Federal Communications Commission updated its TCPA rules requiring “one-to-one consent” which was to become effective Jan. 27, 2025.

The one-to-one consent rule provides that if a business uses an ATDS, artificial or prerecorded voice, the business must obtain prior express consent, one seller at a time.

Thus, it prevents lead generators from using a single consumer’s consent for multiple businesses. Additionally, the one-to-one consent rule provides that the consent must be clear and conspicuous, and the calls and texts initiated pursuant to the consent must be logically and topically associated with the interaction that prompted the consent. This rule applies to both text messages and phone calls.

On Jan. 24, 2025, the FCC postponed the 2023 order by a year, until Jan. 26, 2026. Later that same day the Eleventh Circuit Court of Appeals vacated the 2023 Order, thus eliminating the one-to-one consent rule.

The Eleventh Circuit Court of Appeals held “that the FCC exceeded its statutory authority under the TCPA because the 2023 Order’s new consent restrictions impermissibly conflict[ed] with the ordinary statutory meaning of prior express consent.”

Notably, the court ruled that the FCC exceeded its statutory authority at the outset, when it created the one-to-one consent rule. The court held that the 2023 Order’s one-to-one prior express consent restriction impermissibly conflicted with the ordinary statutory meaning of “prior express consent.” Thus, the Court vacated application of the 2023 Order, and remanded for further proceedings.

As a result, it is very likely that we will see other cases challenging TCPA regulations, especially as to the consent required before making a telemarketing call or text message using an ATDS.

It is unclear whether the FCC will revise its 2023 Order to comply with the Eleventh Circuit’s decision. In order to be prepared for this rule to come into effect, and in an abundance of caution, businesses who use lead generators to source potential consumers’ consent should ascertain that the lead generators are obtaining individual, one-to-one consent.

Businesses should also only contact consumers who provide this consent for telemarketing that is logically and topically associated with that which the consent was provided. Further, in addition to storing consumer contact information, businesses must retain the consent forms, information as to when consent was given, and through whom. Even businesses that do not use lead generators to obtain consent should continue to review their consent practices to ensure strict compliance with the TCPA and mini-TCPAs.

The TCPA requires prior express consent, and in many cases, prior express written consent, for calls and text messages made to prospective consumers. Regardless of any changes to the TCPA, the FTSA still requires that businesses obtain prior express written consent when making unsolicited telephone calls (including sending text messages) using an automated system. And lastly, to further protect your business, the consent form should have robust terms of service, including a class action waiver.

We continue to recommend that businesses ensure compliance with the TCPA, FTSA, and any other state regulations by always obtaining express written consent prior to contacting potential consumers via calls or text messages.

Several leading law firms are looking to take on junior lawyers and trainees from Weil, Gotshal & Manges after its management committee recommended an orderly wind-down of the firm’s global operations. (Photo from Shutterstock)

Several leading law firms are looking to take on junior lawyers and trainees from Weil, Gotshal & Manges after its management committee recommended an orderly wind-down of the firm’s global operations.

Law.com reported Thursday that Sullivan & Cromwell and Paul, Weiss, Rifkind, Wharton & Garrison are speaking with Weil Gotshal’s associates and trainees, and that other firms—including DLA Piper, Simpson Thacher & Bartlett and Latham & Watkins—have varying degrees of interest and engagement. Meanwhile, another source told Law.com that some firms are offering places to prospective trainees who were due to join Weil Gotshal in September.

The wind-down still needs formal approval, with a partnership vote expected this week. Weil Gotshal’s leaders said the recommendation followed a thorough review of alternatives, and sources said partners have begun telling clients that the firm cannot continue. According to Law.com, the firms named were approached for comment.

#7695. Lawyer, business partner accused of defrauding cannabis investor of $750K

A Los Angeles attorney and his business partner are accused of paying for their personal expenses with investor money instead of funding business-to-consumer cannabis trade shows. (Image from Shutterstock)

A Los Angeles attorney and his business partner are accused of paying for their personal expenses with investor money instead of funding business-to-consumer cannabis trade shows, including the unsuccessful Green Street Festival in 2022.

A Los Angeles County court complaint filed by investor Jamie Chisick alleged that attorney Joshua Shelton of the Winston Wolfe Law Firm and his business partner, Rama Mayo, took $750,000 for a 15% ownership stake in the Green Street Symposium.

According to the Oct. 19 complaint, Shelton and Mayo, cannabis entrepreneurs, promised to organize large trade events that would attract thousands of attendees and generate “millions of dollars in revenue,” according to coverage on Law360.

Chisick obtained documents that he said shows that his money had been used for “personal payments, including but not limited to private jets, health insurance, bar dues (Shelton) and general overhead unrelated to GSS operations.”

The 2022 Green Street Festival brought in about $190,000 with about $178,000 refunded. A 2023 festival with projections of attracting over 10,000 attendees and up to $4.7 million in revenue drew a smaller crowd and did not produce a profit.

Chisick seeks to recover his investment and punitive damages, according to the complaint.

#7694. Dems ask SEC, DOL to not issue anti-ESG rules: Exclusive

A coalition of 17 blue state finance officials sent a letter to the agencies to counter prior assertions made by their Republican colleagues.

The Democratic finance officials took particular issue with the Republican officials’ letter relying heavily on a federal judge’s ruling against American Airlines in a lawsuit over the management of its retirement plans. The Republican finance officials used U.S. District Court judge Reed O’Connor’s ruling as evidence that the incorporation of factors like ESG is being used to pursue non-pecuniary goals.

The officials included state auditors, treasurers, controllers and comptrollers from New York City, California, Illinois and 12 other states who said that such a characterization of the use of environmental, social and governance factors is “incorrect and dangerously misleading.”

“The decision in Spence v. American Airlines, which dismissed long-term financial interests as a ‘mere pretext,’ fails to reflect the fundamental reality of long-term investing,” the Democratic officials wrote. “Fiduciaries are not speculators — they are stewards of trillions of dollars in assets that must sustain retirees for decades.”

Officials from Connecticut, Colorado, Delaware, Maryland, Massachusetts, Minnesota, Nevada, New Mexico, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont and Washington also signed onto the letter. They said that risks related to climate change, governance failures and systemic issues are “present-day financial realities affecting market valuations, insurance costs, supply chains and infrastructure resilience."

The Republican officials had said in their Jan. 28 letter that they held “serious concerns” that funds were being used to advance ESG or DEI goals and asked for rulemaking to prohibit plans from using assets to “advance political or social goals.” They also asked the Labor Department and SEC to issue comprehensive guidance explicitly saying that making investment decisions or proxy votes based on ESG or diversity, equity and inclusion objectives is “inconsistent with fiduciary duties.”

Connecticut State Treasurer Erick Russell called the request a “dangerous political proposal” in emailed comments to ESG Dive Wednesday, while Illinois State Treasurer Michael Frerichs went a step further, calling the approach “Orwellian” and “a reckless attempt to put politics ahead of sound financial decision-making” in comments Wednesday.

“Forbidding investment managers from assessing real-world risks — whether they stem from supply chain disruptions, environmental instability, shifting consumer demand, or any other factor — would restrict their ability to fully analyze investment opportunities and inherently runs counter to that fiduciary responsibility,” Russell said.

The blue state fiduciaries warned that if utilizing ESG factors in investment decisions was banned for fiduciaries, it could cause weaker investment performance, create greater exposure to market volatility and increase financial vulnerability for retirees.

“As stewards of public funds, we have a responsibility to ensure that our investments provide stable, long-term returns over periods of decades,” Delaware State Treasurer Colleen Davis told ESG Dive. “It is morally reprehensible and financially negligent to play politics with the American people’s retirement savings and investments.”

Acting SEC Chair Mark Uyeda and Acting Labor Secretary Vince Micone are currently in charge of two agencies who are defending a pair of ESG-linked regulations in court. Uyeda said last week he would seek a delay in arguments in lawsuits about the SEC’s climate-risk disclosure rule, indicating the agency as constructed is not inclined to defend the rule. A federal judge recently ruled in favor of the Biden administration’s Labor Department on its regulation allowing fiduciaries to consider ESG and other collateral benefits in the case of a tiebreaker. Experts expect that both rules are endangered under this Trump administration.

#7688. Head of AI Native Operations at Supabase

Supabase is the Postgres development platform, built by developers for developers. We provide a complete backend solution including Database, Auth, Storage, Edge Functions, Realtime, and Vector Search. All services are deeply integrated and designed for growth.

We are looking for a Head of AI Operations to own how Supabase works.

Supabase is building an AI-native internal operating system: a common way of working across the company where AI carries a meaningful share of the operational load rather than sitting alongside it as an assistant. We are standing up a new central team to build those systems, enable the teams, and embed AI operations throughout the organization. This is the role that runs it.

You will own the maturity model teams are assessed against, the standards that define how work happens here, and the operating cadence, under one design rule: every recurring meeting has to justify why an automated report cannot replace it. You will lead a small team of senior individual contributors, one building the platform and one running enablement.

The premise is that process encoded as agents scales where process enforced by people does not. Your job is to prove that is a repeatable pattern rather than an anomaly, across teams you have no authority over.

We are fully remote and async. The document is the enforcement mechanism here, which means the standards themselves are your deliverable.

Own the maturity model end to end: The rubric, the scoring method, the evidence standard, and the appeals path. Every team ends up with a published assessment and a written plan to its next level.

Run assessments and commitments: Conduct assessments with department heads yourself, landing them as commitments with named owners and dates rather than opinions.

Own the standards layer: Define how work gets tracked, decisions get proposed and resolved, teams migrate onto shared tooling, and stale documentation gets retired. Standards ship as documents teams follow without being chased.

Fix the decision process: Ensure written proposals reach resolution instead of accumulating unresolved by defining stages, exit criteria, and closing mechanisms.

Run the operating cadence: Lead automated weekly reporting, a regular blockers-and-decisions forum, a monthly leadership review, and a quarterly board-level format. Delete meetings a report could replace.

Manage rollouts: Execute private assessments first so leads see only their own and have time to move, followed by a pre-committed public transparency date.

Wire standards into onboarding: Ensure every cohort arrives pre-trained rather than inheriting nearby habits.

Build and direct the team: Hire, grow, review, and direct two senior individual contributors (platform and enablement) without doing their work for them.

Measure and publish outcomes: Measure and publish whether the thesis holds by tracking how much coordination work agents absorb versus what a human program office would cost.

Every standard you write should be the input to something that enforces it, and every enforcement mechanism should produce the evidence that grades it. When you write the rule that work must carry a current status, you are not finished until a report finds the stale items and tells their owners without you in the loop. The same applies to your own function: the team you build gets assessed by the model you own, published next to everyone else's, and you should want that.

The default outcome for a company-wide standard is that teams politely ignore it. So the first question about any standard is not "is this correct" but "what will make people route around this," and the design follows from that answer. Same for meetings: rather than asking what a new sync would accomplish, ask what report would make it unnecessary and build the report. Same for the public transparency date: it gets committed before anyone has a score to defend, because afterwards the lobbying is rational.

You direct agents rather than doing the work by hand, and you can tell whether the direction was any good. That means reading an agent workflow definition and knowing the procedure is too broad, reading a data model and challenging the metric behind it, reading a pull request from your own team and sending it back. Your working artifacts are files in version control that agents can read, not chat transcripts. You will not build the platform. You will be the person who says whether what got built is right.

Scale & Cadence Experience: Have run operating cadence and program discipline at a company crossing ~200 to 800 people while remote and async.

Agentic AI Expertise: Have personally built agentic AI workflows that others depended on. You can read/review an agent workflow definition, a data model, and a pull request to judge quality.

Standard Adoption Track Record: Have taken a standard from zero to company-wide without direct authority over adopters, with a clear mechanism that made it stick.

Async Communication Skills: Are an exceptional writer who leverages documents as enforcement mechanisms.

Accountability: Are comfortable being graded publicly by the system you build alongside every other team.

Have run a maturity model or capability assessment across teams you did not own, published results, and driven organizational reallocations.

Are native to Git, Markdown, and Pull Requests (whether through engineering or technical operations background).

Have permanently eliminated a recurring meeting by replacing it with an automated system.

Deep software engineering background is a plus, but not required.

Standards land without chasing: Rules are written, published, wired into onboarding, and followed because non-compliance is automatically visible.

Universal coverage: Every team has an evidence-backed assessment, owner, and written path to the next level, with disagreements handled through published appeal channels.

Firm transparency dates: Assessments transition from private to public on pre-committed dates without exception.

Net-negative meeting time: By year end, the operating rhythm consumes less calendar time across the organization than when you arrived.

Autonomous operational function: Your two reports operate independently against written charters, at least one non-reference team runs a genuinely automated production workflow, and you focus on review rather than execution.

We hire globally. We believe you can do your best work from anywhere. There are no Supabase offices, but we provide a WeWork membership or co-working allowance you can use anywhere in the world.

Every team member receives ESOP (equity ownership) in the company. We want everyone to share in the upside of what we’re building together.

Use this budget to set up your ideal work environment—laptop, monitor, headphones, or whatever helps you do your best work.

Supabase covers 100% of health insurance for employees and 80% for dependents, wherever you are. Your wellbeing and your family’s health are important to us.

Once a year, the entire company gathers in a new city for a week of connection, collaboration, and fun. It’s a highlight of our year.

We operate asynchronously and trust you to manage your own time. You know what needs to be done and when.

Every team member receives an annual education allowance to spend on learning—courses, books, conferences, or anything that supports your growth.

Supabase was born-remote and open-source-first. We believe our globally distributed team is our secret weapon in building tools developers love.

Over $1B raised (including our $500M Series F)

We move fast, build in public, and use what we ship. If it’s in your project, we probably use it in ours too. We believe deeply in the open-source ecosystem and strive to support—not replace—existing tools and communities.

#7687. Graduate Software Engineer, Open Source and Linux, Canonical Ubuntu at Canonical

Canonical is a leading provider of open source software and operating systems to the global enterprise and technology markets. Our platform, Ubuntu, is very widely used in breakthrough enterprise initiatives such as public cloud, data science, AI, engineering innovation, and IoT. Our customers include the world's leading public cloud and silicon providers, and industry leaders in many sectors. The company is a pioneer of global distributed collaboration, with 1200+ colleagues in 75+ countries and very few office-based roles. Teams meet two to four times yearly in person, in interesting locations around the world, to align on strategy and execution.

The company is founder led, profitable and growing.

We are hiring 2025 and 2026 Graduate Software Engineers into engineering teams around the world. As a global platform company we offer a wide range of software engineering challenges, in both open source products and commercial business systems. We have teams that work in a variety of languages, typically Python, Golang, Rust, C/C++, JavaScript and of course... Bash. We work from the very lowest levels of the Linux system - BIOS and boot loaders, firmware, kernel and drivers, all the way up to desktop applications and containers. We work on tiny devices like the Raspberry Pi and new RISC-V boards, all the way up to supercomputers, clouds and Kubernetes clusters. We work on compilers and toolchains, and we work on security, cryptography, performance and documentation. Some of our teams focus on packaging thousands of pieces of software, others focus on deep contributions to a single body of code.

If you are excited about the potential that open source has for humanity and the enterprise, you have outstanding results in your academic career, and you are excited to contribute to the open source stack, this is the best way to apply to Canonical. We will work with you to identify teams and projects that would be interesting and a good fit for your skills and motivations. The process is highly competitive, it will require effort and excellence to succeed if you apply here.

Most of our engineering teams work from home. We try to align a single team in a single time zone - EMEA (Europe, Middle East and Africa), APAC (Asia Pacific and Indian Ocean), and AMER (North, South and Central Americas). Even though you work from home, we try to ensure you always have colleagues alongside to coach and mentor you, and for the companionship of shared problem solving and pair programming. Larger projects have multiple teams and might span the globe. We work with the open source community and specialize in building teams that work well in the 'fishbowl' of open source engineering. This is full time work, five days a week, often solving hard problems with significant responsibility. We don't generally work weekends and nights and we do enjoy good holidays but we also expect productive and intense engagement Monday to Friday.

We bring all our engineering teams together in person twice a year for a deep 'sprint' with other teams to stimulate discussion and enable a wide range of career development paths. This is a fantastic way to demonstrate and develop your skill in software, learn about a wide range of technologies, make a meaningful impact to open source, and see some very interesting new cities that you might never otherwise get to visit.

If you find the open source stack amazing, and you have been a consistent high-performing student in your school and university, then this will be a challenging and exciting start to your career.

Location: This is a Globally remote role.

We consider geographical location, experience, and performance in shaping compensation worldwide. We revisit compensation annually (and more often for graduates and associates) to ensure we recognize outstanding performance. In addition to base pay, we offer a performance-driven annual bonus or commission. We provide all team members with additional benefits which reflect our values and ideals. We balance our programs to meet local needs and ensure fairness globally.

Canonical is a pioneering tech firm at the forefront of the global move to open source. As the company that publishes Ubuntu, one of the most important open source projects and the platform for AI, IoT and the cloud, we are changing the world of software. We recruit on a global basis and set a very high standard for people joining the company. We expect excellence - in order to succeed, we need to be the best at what we do. Most colleagues at Canonical have worked from home since its inception in 2004.​ Working here is a step into the future, and will challenge you to think differently, work smarter, learn new skills, and raise your game.

We are proud to foster a workplace free from discrimination. Diversity of experience, perspectives, and background create a better work environment and better products. Whatever your identity, we will give your application fair consideration.

#7685. Judge accused of making racial remarks, skipping court is no-show at her own hearing

U.S. District Judge Ada Brown of the Northern District of Texas failed to show up to a hearing Friday to address misconduct allegations. (Photo from Facebook/Judge Ada Brown for SCOTUS)

A federal judge in Dallas—accused of refusing to take cases, making racial insults and abandoning the bench—has failed to appear at an investigatory hearing about the allegations.

U.S. District Judge Ada Brown of the Northern District of Texas did not show up Friday for a judicial committee hearing regarding concerns that a mental condition may be interfering with her ability to perform her duties, Law360 reports.

A three-judge special committee of the judicial council of the 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals at New Orleans met Friday morning to address two complaints against Brown. When she did not arrive, the committee paused for 30 minutes to give her more time but ended the proceedings without her.

Brown is accused of delaying rulings on motions, closing cases with pending motions, recusing herself from cases for unusual reasons, making “racial insults,” sending “bizarre” emails to colleagues in the middle of the night, and failing to come to work, according to documents released by the 5th Circuit’s judicial council.

Law360 attempted Friday to reach an assistant in Brown’s office but had not received a response.

Racial comments to attorney sparked investigation of federal judge

ProcessOS is a new kind of Camunda product: business processes described in natural language, generated as executable BPMN workflows, and improved autonomously from production data. We’re hiring the first cohort of Forward Deployed Engineers to bring it into production at enterprise customers. You’ll own the deployment journey from first process file to a working, improving system, and hand off a functioning capability to the customer’s team. The code you write and the patterns you discover feed directly back into how ProcessOS is built. This is a rare opportunity to shape a product, a function, and a field practice from day one.

You’ll work end‑to‑end across Java services and React interfaces, collaborating closely with a talented global team to measure, improve, and scale performance and fault tolerance in real-world distributed systems.

Deploy and prove. Own the journey from first process file to production workflow. At 90 days: at least one workflow running, the improvement loop active, and measurable fitness gains the customer can see. At 12 months: 3–5 customers with viable deployments.

Work at depth technically. Configure and run Camunda clusters locally and in cloud environments. Debug integration failures. Build custom agents where platform defaults don’t fit. Write connector logic that gets legacy enterprise systems talking to ProcessOS.

Build the playbook. There is no deployment template yet. Document what good looks like as you discover it, and make the next implementation faster.

Feed the product. Custom agents you write get contributed back. Integration patterns get codified. Production bugs you find, you often fix. Your field work is a direct input to ProcessOS.

Hand off deliberately. Leave customers with a team that can operate independently, is trained on the platform, and acts on improvement results without you.

Comfort with ambiguity: you make sound judgment calls without a playbook and document what you learn.
