#7625. Is Montgomery affirmative action’s final chapter?

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

On Oct. 19, the Supreme Court granted cert in a case called Association for Education Fairness v. Montgomery County Board of Education. I am surprised it hasn’t received more press coverage because it could be the final nail in affirmative action’s coffin.

Perhaps you think the Supreme Court already hammered in that nail in Students for Fair Admissions, Inc. v. President & Fellows of Harvard College, but you’d be wrong. In that case, the court found racial preferences at Harvard and the University of North Carolina to be illegal. Nevertheless, many scholars are now urging schools to turn to what I call “race neutral affirmative action.” These are programs that seek to increase the number of some racial groups relative to others not by selecting for race itself, but by selecting for characteristics correlated with race. For example, instead of using race preferences in admissions, a university uses preferences for applicants who live in zip codes that are nearly all black, applicants who grew up on Indian reservations, or applicants for whom English is a second language. These are real-life examples of what some universities have done when they were forbidden from using race. Many affirmative action supporters think these sorts of things are perfectly legal.

But I have long argued that race proxies are just as illegal as using race itself. My arguments became moot points after the Supreme Court allowed universities to use race itself in admissions in the 2003 case of Grutter v. Bollinger. But now that SFFA has taken that off the table, the question I teed up is back in the limelight: is it constitutional to use racial proxies instead?

That’s what Montgomery County allegedly did to pick the students for its magnet middle schools. Its efforts predated SFFA because, even before the Supreme Court told universities not to use race, they had told school districts not to. In a nutshell, the alleged facts are these: Asian children make up only 15% of the school system’s population – it is majority black and Hispanic – but were taking up half the spots in the magnet middle schools. This didn’t go over well with many parents, so the school board sought to even things out. The board tried several plans but ultimately used a lottery among the applicants who scored above the 85th percentile in their neighborhood on standardized tests. Because the pool was based on how well applicants did compared only to others in their own neighborhood, the plan spread magnet school spots across the county – and, because many neighborhoods don’t have much racial diversity, it spread the spots across the races, too. The number of black and Latino students went up and the number of Asian students went down.

According to Supreme Court precedent, this is unconstitutional. We have a long history of attempts to discriminate indirectly when we couldn’t discriminate directly – and we have an equally long history of the Supreme Court telling us it’s illegal. For example, when we couldn’t deny the ability to vote on the basis of race, we tried using literacy tests and grandfather clauses and felon disenfranchisement instead. The court said those things are illegal. When we couldn’t segregate schools, we tried drawing school district boundaries around mostly black neighborhoods and mostly white neighborhoods instead. The court said we can’t do that, either.

The doctrine is this: if your “purpose” is to discriminate on the basis of race and your “effect” is to discriminate on the basis of race, then you are engaged in discrimination on the basis of race – even if you aren’t using a racial classification. It’s something like the old adage: if something walks like a duck and quacks like a duck, it’s a duck.

Most scholars supported these precedents when people were discriminating against blacks. But now not so much. Thus, I expect a bevy of amicus briefs from academics contorting their way through them. But the contortions I have seen thus far are very weak. For example, the leading theory on why these precedents don’t doom Montgomery County is the old distinction between “benign” and “invidious” discrimination: the purpose to help is different than the purpose to hurt. The precedents involved the purpose to hurt blacks, whereas Montgomery County was trying to help blacks (and Latinos); hurting Asians was just a byproduct, not the purpose.

If you thought the Supreme Court had already rejected – over and over again – the distinction between “benign” and “invidious” discrimination, you’d be right. After all, that’s how we got SFFA. As the court explained there, life is often zero-sum: if you help one race by giving them more spots, you necessarily hurt other races by giving them fewer spots. What is “benign” for one is “invidious” for the others. It’s a distinction without a difference.

The scholars say the cases rejecting the benign-invidious distinction don’t count because they involved racial classifications, not racial proxies. But the court in SFFA anticipated this move and cut it off: “[U]niversities may not simply establish through . . . other means the regime we hold unlawful today. … [W]hat cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly. … The Constitution deals with substance, not shadows.” Yes, that’s dicta, but isn’t it very, very probative of what the very same justices will think about the very same question next year?

Moreover, the dicta didn’t come from nowhere: in fact, the Supreme Court has already struck down “benign” racial proxies – a bunch of them. When governments engage in racial gerrymandering of voting districts, they don’t use racial classifications: voters are assigned to one district or another based on where they live, not their skin color. Yet, even when these gerrymanders have been designed to help black and Latino voters, the Supreme Court has struck them down all the same, including just this past term in Louisiana v. Callais. Is not Montgomery County engaged in gerrymandering no less than Louisiana? It’s just school districts, not voting districts.

It is true that the court has required discriminators to try “race-neutral alternatives” before they can use race itself. But the court requires race-neutral alternatives only when discriminators otherwise have a compelling interest to justify their discrimination. All this means is that the court prefers racial proxies to racial classifications when forced to choose; it doesn’t mean racial proxies are insulated from constitutional scrutiny.

Still, the court may not need to get into all this because the question presented in the Montgomery County case merely asks what counts as a discriminatory “effect.” The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit held that the Asian students had to show a “disparate impact” – a term borrowed from Title VII law that means the challenged practice impacts one race more than another – and they couldn’t do so because, even after the gerrymandering, they still comprised a greater portion of the magnet school spots than they did of magnet school applicants.

Although it is true that disparate impact is one way to show a racial effect under the Supreme Court’s purpose-and-effect precedents, as I previously explained, it is not the only way. For example, when the Supreme Court said that school districts couldn’t evade its desegregation decrees by drawing district lines around mostly white neighborhoods and mostly black neighborhoods, it did not require the plaintiffs to show a disparate impact (e.g., schools of different quality); it was enough that one school was overwhelmingly white and the other was overwhelmingly black. When the Supreme Court has said that legislatures couldn’t gerrymander voting districts, it did not require the plaintiffs to show a disparate impact (e.g., differential vote dilution); it was enough that the racial composition of the districts had been affected.

It is true that what exactly the racial effect is in the voting cases is undertheorized. There is no obvious baseline to compare to the gerrymandered district lines in order to measure the “effect.” For this reason, some scholars think the court has all but read out the effect requirement from the purpose-and-effect test. Maybe so. The effect requirement comes from an old case called Palmer v. Thompson: there, Jackson, Mississippi, closed all their public swimming pools rather than desegregate them; the court held that this wasn’t unconstitutional racial discrimination because all the races had been affected equally. The ruling is unpopular among scholars on the left; law professor Randall Kennedy at Harvard has compared it to Korematsu. Thus, I doubt many will mourn its demise; plaintiffs would still have to show an injury to establish standing in federal court. But overruling it will only help the plaintiffs in the Montgomery County case.

Still, a lingering question that hasn’t been asked enough is whether the purpose-and-effect doctrine – or even a purpose-only doctrine if Palmer goes away – is consistent with the original understanding of the Constitution. It is hard for me to see how it couldn’t be: it is very easy to evade any rule by proxy; surely, they knew that even back in 1868. But I haven’t seen any historical analyses yet. I hope there are some in the briefing.

I appreciate that for many scholars it is inconceivable that we could end up in a world where it is illegal to do anything about racial disparities. Many of them endorse so-called “antiracism” and believe that all racial disparities must be the product of racism – and, indeed, that we, too, are racists if we don’t do something about them. This means we can sometimes have “too many” Asians. Maybe they’re right about that, maybe they’re wrong. But the 14th Amendment does not enact Mr. Ibram X. Kendi’s “How to Be an Antiracist.”

Brian Fitzpatrick was a law clerk to Antonin Scalia and is currently the Milton R. Underwood Chair in Free Enterprise and Professor of Law at Vanderbilt Law School.

#7624. New York State Bar Association tells lawyers not to bill for time saved by AI

The New York State Bar Association is calling for restrictions on how much lawyers can bill clients for the amount of time saved using artificial intelligence tools or expended learning how to use it. (Image from Shutterstock)

The New York State Bar Association is calling for restrictions on how much lawyers can bill clients for the amount of time saved using artificial intelligence tools or expended learning how to use it.

Law360 reported Monday that the state bar association’s Committee on Artificial Intelligence and Emerging Technologies issued a report classifying the cost of buying and maintaining such software as an overhead expense that can be passed along as a disbursement only when tied to a specific client matter and when the basis for the charge has been disclosed.

According to Law360, the report added that lawyers generally don’t have to tell clients about AI use for administrative tasks—such as word processing, spelling and grammar checks, calendaring or timekeeping—provided that the use doesn’t affect fees.

“Generative AI is indelibly changing the practice of law. As part of our mission to be the leading voice for the legal profession, we are providing clear guidelines on the use of AI tools as a resource, so attorneys can use AI responsibly and ethically in their practices,” said Taa Grays, the president of the New York State Bar Association, in a statement. “The guidelines can help attorneys avoid possible perils of using AI, including inadvertently practicing law in a jurisdiction where they are not licensed or failing to notify clients or the courts of AI use.”

The committee also flagged familiar hazards, such as biased training data that may deepen existing inequities. Confidentiality is another concern: If an AI tool learns from one client’s information in a way that makes it available in another client’s matter, lawyers must turn to the New York Rules of Professional Conduct.

The report cautioned against building tools that deliver automated legal services in ways that could amount to unauthorized practice or using AI to pass as a human with prospective clients.

Supervising lawyers were reminded that they remain responsible for their subordinates’ compliance and should not assume that a law firm-approved tool or policy removes the need to review work on each matter.

According to Law360, the state bar association’s governing body adopted the report Saturday.

The fate of billable hours is in the hands of artificial intelligence

#7622. Supreme Court declines Trump administration's request to intervene in California ballot dispute

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

The Trump administration on Monday morning asked the Supreme Court to intervene in its efforts to keep California from counting ballots cast by what it contends are more than 20,000 noncitizens who have registered to vote in that state. In a brief, unsigned order released to reporters shortly before 6 p.m., however, the court turned down the government's request. There were no noted dissents.

In a 19-page filing, U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer requested an order from the justices that would require California to keep those ballots separate until the voters’ citizenship could be verified. “Once California commingles the challenged ballots with lawful ones,” Sauer wrote, “there is no way to get the challenged ballots back.”

The filing was the latest chapter in the Trump administration’s push to combat alleged voter fraud. It began last month, when the administration went to federal court in Los Angeles, seeking an order directing the state not to send ballots to, or count the ballots of, voters who were likely not citizens.

On Oct. 28, U.S. District Judge David Carter turned down the government’s request for a temporary order directing California to sequester the ballots of “likely noncitizens.” Among other things, he questioned the credibility of the Trump administration’s allegations that the voters it had identified were not U.S. citizens. On Friday, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit also rejected the Trump administration’s motion for emergency relief.

With the midterm elections now just one day away, the Trump administration sought relief next in the Supreme Court. Sauer argued that the government is likely to prevail on the merits of its claim – a key factor that courts consider in deciding whether to grant temporary relief – because federal law bars anyone who is not a U.S. citizen from voting in federal elections. Therefore, he wrote, “it follows that any ballot cast by an alien is unlawful” and states cannot count them.

The United States will also suffer permanent harm (another factor that courts consider in deciding whether to award temporary relief), Sauer continued, because “‘California admits that there is no way to trace a ballot after it is processed.’” The government’s “injury will continue to mount,” Sauer contended, “through Tuesday, November 10 (a week after election day, California’s deadline for receiving mail ballots.)”

By contrast, Sauer said, California will not suffer “undue hardship” from having to sequester the ballots at issue in this case. Indeed, he suggested, “California’s own election laws contemplate the segregation of challenged ballots, and the segregation of challenged ballots is a standard remedy in election cases.”

Sauer asked the court to also issue an immediate temporary order, known as an administrative injunction, “that requires California to segregate mail ballots from persons whom the United States has identified as likely noncitizens” while the justices consider the government’s request.

The Trump administration’s filing went first to Justice Elena Kagan, who has primary responsibility for emergency appeals from the 9th Circuit. Kagan then referred it to the full court, which declined the Trump administration’s request.

Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

#7617. Court won’t intervene in California ballot dispute

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

It’s Election Day in the United States. At SCOTUSblog, we’ll be watching not only for race results, but also for new voting-related legal battles. In recent weeks, the Supreme Court has addressed several emergency applications linked to the midterms, and the justices received – and decided – another one on Monday on alleged noncitizen voting in California.

On Monday, the Trump administration returned to the Supreme Court’s interim docket, asking the justices to intervene in its efforts to keep California from counting ballots cast by what it contends are noncitizen voters. Just hours later, the court denied the request. There were no noted dissents. For more on the dispute, see the On Site section below.

Also on Monday, the justices heard argument in two cases: Maxwell v. Dinis, on a federal inmate’s ability to use a habeas statute, 28 U.S.C. § 2241, to contest the Federal Bureau of Prisons’ refusal to accelerate his transfer to a halfway house or home confinement; and Younge v. Fulton Judicial Circuit District Attorney’s Office, Georgia, on whether an affirmative defense may be asserted as a basis for summary judgment if not presented earlier in a pleading.

On Monday afternoon, the court released its calendar for the January argument session, which will begin on Monday, Jan. 11. Learn about the session in the On Site section.

Today, the justices will hear argument in St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy, a religious discrimination challenge brought by Catholic preschools in Colorado over the state’s requirement that all schools participating in its universal preschool program must admit everyone – including LGBTQ children and children with LGBTQ parents.

Tomorrow, the justices will hear argument in Guerrero v. Johnson, on the limited circumstances in which a state prisoner can return to federal court for a second round of post-conviction review.

On Oct. 21, the Trump administration asked the justices to allow it to resume construction of its border wall in the Big Bend region of southwestern Texas. The request is now fully briefed, and the court’s decision could come at any time.

Kelsey Dallas is SCOTUSblog's managing editor and the primary author of the SCOTUStoday newsletter.

#7615. The border wall dispute isn’t fit for the emergency docket

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

In its latest request to the Supreme Court over President Donald Trump’s approach to immigration, the Justice Department turned to the court’s emergency docket to ask for fast-track permission to construct a border barrier system along a 517-mile stretch in remote west Texas. Stymied by a federal district court’s preliminary injunction issued in October, the Justice Department argues that Supreme Court intervention is needed to prevent irreparable harm to the country. But details of the government’s legal argument reveal that the Trump administration hopes to use the emergency docket as a fast track to victory regardless of the actual urgency of the legal dispute.

Early this year, the Department of Homeland Security began taking important preliminary steps to build physical barriers through Big Bend National Park, Big Bend Ranch State Park, and nearby property along the U.S.-Mexico border. Part of the Border Patrol’s Big Bend Sector, covering approximately one-quarter of the entire border, no artificial barriers exist there. Despite its massive geographic reach, the region is sparsely populated and at immense distance from large urban centers. Unlike other parts of the U.S.-Mexico border, few people or goods cross from one country to the other in the Big Bend Sector. Indeed, according to U.S. District Judge Kathleen Cardone, who issued a preliminary injunction blocking DHS from carrying out its plans to erect a border barrier in the area, this is the border region with “the lowest aggregate number of apprehensions [of migrants] and the lowest number of apprehensions per mile of border.”

In Mullin v. Friends of the Ruidosa Church, a group of individuals with personal or business ties to the region, along with two advocacy groups, argued that DHS had failed to comply with required environmental reviews. Pointing to a 1996 law signed by President Bill Clinton, the Justice Department responded that Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin and his predecessor, Kristi Noem, waived application of those environmental laws. The government also argued that the district court lacked the power to decide the lawsuit in the first place.

Cardone disagreed with the government on both counts. Congress narrowed courts’ jurisdiction in border-barrier disputes, but left room for courts to consider constitutional challenges to DHS’s conduct, she concluded. The challenge to Mullin’s waiver of environmental laws raises a constitutional question, Cardone added.

Having concluded that she could consider the challengers’ lawsuit, Cardone then turned to the criteria that Congress imposed on the secretary of Homeland Security to waive environmental review. The 1996 law directs the immigration agency “to waive all legal requirements” that could slow or impede construction of border barriers and roads. But the same law also instructs DHS to build barriers and roads “in areas of high illegal entry into the United States.” Considering the government’s data about apprehensions of people and seizures of drugs in the Big Bend Sector, as compared to other parts of the U.S.-Mexico border, Cardone concluded that the region cannot be considered to have high levels of illegal entry. “[I]f the Big Bend Sector is an area of high illegal entry, so is every other sector,” Cardone announced.

Seven days after Cardone released her opinion, the U.S. solicitor general asked the Supreme Court to intervene. Much of the government’s argument turns on its disagreement with Cardone about what constitutes an area of “high illegal entry.” Mullin determined that the Big Bend Sector constitutes an area of high illegal entry because Customs and Border Protection, the DHS agency that enforces immigration laws at and near the border, apprehended 89,000 people and “seized enormous amounts” of illicit drugs from fiscal years 2021 to 2025, the government explains. In addition, failure to build a border barrier in this region “would act as a dangerous magnet” for additional illegal entries, the solicitor general claims. Despite Mullin’s assessment that the facts on the ground met the “high illegal entry” threshold required by Congress, “the district court nonetheless issued an unprecedented injunction blocking those waivers and halting associated border-wall construction,” the solicitor general wrote to the court.

Unsurprisingly, the challengers disagree. Opposing the government’s request for relief from the justices, they describe Mullin and Noem’s waivers as “unprecedented” and claim they “carry undisputed and extraordinary political and economic significance.”

The solicitor general’s claim is fundamentally a dispute about the proper interpretation of the text of the 1996 law. The government argues that courts cannot second-guess Mullin’s decision to waive environmental laws, and that Mullin’s view of what constitutes “high illegal entry” is all that matters. Cardone disagrees and contends that courts have a role to play here.

By turning to the emergency docket, the Justice Department has dispensed with the ordinary appellate process in favor of a fast-track path to, it hopes, final victory. Wanting an answer sooner rather than later is understandable, but a party’s interest in “line-jumping,” as Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson has described the emergency docket, isn’t reason enough to circumvent the slower course of the ordinary appellate process. Jackson would prefer to limit the emergency docket to situations in which an actual emergency exists. It’s hard to see what exigency exists in west Texas, however. The solicitor general argues that drugs and people will continue to enter through the Big Bend Sector. That is undoubtedly true, but, as that stretch of land has been unfortified since it became a border on March 18, 1848, nothing is likely to occur in the near future that is markedly different from past decades.

The government’s request for fast-track intervention by the Supreme Court also does not meet the standards set by Jackson’s ideological opposites. Explaining his view of the court’s emergency docket in Trump v. CASA, the court’s fast-track decision announcing that district courts are not authorized to issue universal injunctions, Justice Brett Kavanaugh wrote that its alternative pathway is appropriate when “Congress passes a major new statute, or the Executive Branch issues a major new rule or executive order.” Neither applies to the border-wall dispute. Congress enacted the contested statute 30 years ago and the waivers issued by Mullin and Noem are neither an agency rule nor an executive order.

Nor is the border-wall legal battle the type of dispute that only the Supreme Court can resolve. In a 2021 speech, Justice Samuel Alito compared the court’s emergency docket to a hospital’s emergency room, suggesting that, in his view at least, the fast-track process is proper only when no suitable alternative exists. But an alternative does exist to decide if Cardone overstepped. The government could have appealed Cardone’s decision to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit. Like other circuit courts, the 5th Circuit regularly reviews preliminary injunctions granted by district courts. As Kavanaugh explained in CASA, “The courts of appeals and this Court can (and regularly do) expeditiously review district court decisions awarding or denying preliminary injunctive relief.” Instead of asking the 5th Circuit to correct the mistake it claims Cardone committed, the solicitor general skipped the 5th Circuit and went directly to the Supreme Court.

The reason it did this is not difficult to figure out: The administration is hopeful that it will receive a friendly audience at the Supreme Court. But this is a fast-track procedure meant for exceptional circumstances. And there is nothing exceptional about the legal fight over the administration’s attempt to build new segments of border barrier in rural west Texas. If the court grants the government’s request to pause Cardone’s preliminary injunction, allowing construction to move forward where no barrier currently exists, it should, at the very least, explain how this case meets the criteria that the justices have previously provided and if the term “emergency docket” is a misnomer.

César Cuauhtémoc García Hernández is the author of three books about immigration law and policy.

#7612. Will an ability to hold federal officers accountable survive this term?

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

At a time when there is a desire to hold ICE agents accountable for their constitutional violations, the Supreme Court might be poised to eliminate the only way to hold them civilly liable under federal law.

By way of background, if state or local officers violate the Constitution, they can be sued under a federal statute, 42 U.S.C. Section 1983. But no federal law authorizes suits against federal officers for constitutional violations. Rather, the ability to sue a federal government officer for money damages comes from a 1971 Supreme Court decision, Bivens v. Six Unknown Named Agents of the Federal Bureau of Narcotics. There, the court said that it would allow a cause of action for money damages under the Fourth Amendment even without a federal statute authorizing it.

Nevertheless, for decades, the Supreme Court has refused to extend or even apply Bivens to other violations of constitutional rights by federal officers, and several conservative justices have called for it to be overruled. Now, in Nielsen v. Watanabe, to be argued on Nov. 9, the court will again confront whether to allow a Bivens suit – and perhaps whether to end such claims entirely.

The underlying issue is about separation of powers: should the court provide a remedy for constitutional violations or is that entirely the province of Congress? But it also is about accountability: without Bivens, how can those who violate constitutional rights, including ICE agents, be held responsible and how can those injured be compensated?

Webster Bivens alleged that he had been subjected to an illegal and humiliating search by agents of the Federal Bureau of Narcotics. Bivens sought money damages as compensation for the harms he suffered. The court held that a federal law cause of action for money damages could be inferred directly from the Fourth Amendment. The majority, in an opinion by Justice William Brennan, emphasized that individuals whose rights have been violated should not be relegated to state law remedies, which might be inadequate or hostile to the federal constitutional interest.

In an important and often-cited concurring opinion, Justice John Marshall Harlan explained that the federal courts long have devised remedies for violations of federal law. Harlan said that it is essential that federal courts be able to provide such relief because “it is apparent that some form of damages is the only possible remedy for someone in Bivens’ alleged position. … For people in Bivens’ shoes, it is damages or nothing.” Harlan rejected the claim that the court violates separation of powers when it creates such a cause of action and remedy. In his view, the court is responsible for upholding and enforcing the Bill of Rights, and, hence, the judiciary need not wait for the legislature in order to act.

Chief Justice Warren Burger and Justices Hugo Black and Harry Blackmun dissented. Each wrote an opinion arguing that separation of powers means that Congress, and not the court, should create a cause of action for damages against federal officers. Black explained that “[s]hould the time come when Congress desires such lawsuits, it has before it a model of valid legislation, 42 U.S.C. §1983, to create a damage remedy against federal officers.” Similarly, Blackmun argued that “it is the Congress, and not this Court, that should act.”

For a decade after Bivens, the court applied and extended it. In 1979’s Davis v. Passman, the court allowed a Bivens suit under the due process clause of the Fifth Amendment for an equal protection claim. Congressman Otto Passman fired his administrative assistant, Shirley Davis, because he wanted a male to fill the position. In allowing the suit against the congressman, the court emphasized the judiciary's role in ensuring effective protection of constitutional rights.

And only a year later, in Carlson v. Green, the court allowed a Bivens suit for violation of the Eighth Amendment. A mother sued federal prison officials on behalf of her deceased son, claiming that he was the victim of gross inadequacies of medical facilities and staff, which caused his death and constituted cruel and unusual punishment. A remedy was available under the Federal Tort Claims Act; thus, the issue before the court was whether a Bivens suit should be allowed in light of this alternative. The court concluded that Bivens suits were a “counterpart” to the Federal Tort Claims Act because the act creates liability for the federal government and a Bivens cause of action permits recovery from federal officers themselves. The court found no indication that Congress intended for the act to preclude Bivens suits.

Since 1980, however, the court has not ruled in favor of a Bivens claim. In its most recent decision about Bivens, 2022’s Egbert v. Boule, the court noted that it had “declined 11 times to imply a similar cause of action for other alleged constitutional violations” and that “in all but the most unusual circumstances, prescribing a cause of action is a job for Congress, not the courts.”

Specifically, the court has held that that such claims are not allowed if there is a statute that precludes suits (in 2010’s Hui v. Castaneda), or that provides an alternative remedy even if it is inadequate (in 1988’s Schweiker v. Chilicky). It has precluded Bivens claims for those injured while in the military, even for egregious violations of their rights (in 1987’s United States v. Stanley). It has ruled that Bivens suits should be allowed only if they are on balance desirable and consistently has found that they are not (in 2007’s Wilkie v. Robbins, 2017’s Ziglar v. Abbasi, 2020’s Hernandez v. Mesa, and Boule). And it has precluded Bivens suits against private prisons that contract with the federal government (in 2001’s Correctional Services Corp. v. Malesko) and the guards employed by them (in 2012’s Minecci v. Pollard).

Based on this line of cases, the court in Egbert v. Boule stressed that recognizing a Bivens cause of action “is ‘a disfavored judicial activity.’” The court stated that

The court then laid out the framework for Bivens claims going forward. According to the majority, this should be guided by a two-step inquiry:

This is a test that puts a very strong presumption against recognizing Bivens claims.

Like Carlson v. Green, Nielsen v. Watanabe involves an Eighth Amendment claim for cruel and unusual punishment.The case involves a prisoner, Kekai Watanabe, who alleges that he suffered a broken tailbone when attacked by other prisoners that caused him excruciating pain and that a staff nurse, Francis Nielsen, denied him medical care. The court granted review as to whether the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit “erred [here] in recognizing a Bivens cause of action.”

Watanabe argues to the court that this case is governed by Carlson v. Green and does not seek to extend Bivens in any way. His brief states: “Watanabe asserts the same kind of violation of the same constitutional right by the same type of defendant in the same institutional setting pursuant to the same substantive standards as the plaintiff in Carlson. This is precisely the kind of claim this Court has long understood Carlson to encompass.”

In response, Nielsen argues that Bivens suits are strongly disfavored and that there are “significant factual differences such as the immediacy and severity of the harm alleged” compared with Carlson. But that is not all: Nielsen also expressly argues that “Bivens should be overruled” and that “Congress, not the judiciary, creates causes of action.”

The court could affirm the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit and allow a Bivens suit, saying that this is governed by Carlson. Or the court could distinguish Carlson, accepting Nielsen’s argument that there are sufficient factual differences between the cases, essentially limiting Bivens claims only for cruel and unusual punishment claims involving deaths. Or the court could overrule Carlson but not overrule Bivens.

Or the court could overrule Bivens entirely, which several conservative justices have advocated in the past.

The fundamental disagreement, as it was in Bivens, is whether it is the judicial role to provide remedies for violations of constitutional rights or whether that is just for Congress. The practical reality is that without Bivens suits, those whose rights have been violated – even horribly – are left with no recourse. In Hernandez v. Mesa, for example, a boy in Mexico was killed by shot fired across the border by a federal agent in Texas. The court’s rejection of a Bivens suit left no remedy at all.

In that case, and in many other situations, the Federal Tort Claims Act does not allow suits against the United States. Often there are not state tort remedies available either. To paraphrase Justice Harlan, for people in the shoes of many injured by federal officers, it is Bivens suits or nothing.

I would like to think that the reports of egregious constitutional violations by ICE agents, including killings, would cause the court to realize the importance of Bivens suits and to not end such causes of action. That is what makes Nielsen v. Watanabe so important.

Erwin Chemerinsky is the Dean and Jesse H. Choper Distinguished Professor of Law, University of California, Berkeley School of Law.

#7611. Smart Acquisition Or Frankenstack? Stagwell-Freestar And DoorDash-Instacart

It’s fall, and M&A is in the air. Two acquisitions happened this week: Stagwell bought Freestar, and DoorDash agreed to buy Instacart.

Here at AdExchanger, we’re always intrigued by the rationale for acquisitions – from the ones that feel like yin meeting yang to the ones that feel more like stitching together a Frankenstack. (Had to get a spooky reference in!)

In the first half of the podcast, we discuss Stagwell buying Freestar. Why would an indie agency want to build a company that helps open web publishers better set up their ad stacks? Our managing editor, Anthony Vargas, who covered the acquisition, talks about the hints the companies dropped, including how Freestar’s 1,000 publisher site connections could support Stagwell’s principal media business. Are we seeing a rehash of GroupM buying ad network 24/7 Real Media – 19 years later?

Then, when retailers merge, could the extremely fragmented retail media space defragment just a bit? At the time of the recording, DoorDash was in advanced talks to buy Instacart – and on Thursday, news dropped that the acquisition was official.

Pending approval, DoorDash Ads and Instacart’s Carrot Ads will likely come together. Carrot Ads also offers a white-labeled retail media business, which recently added Gopuff as a customer. So imagine Russian nesting dolls, or that image of a whale eating a shark eating a fish – because this type of M&A is going to change how marketers work with retail media companies, which our senior editor, James Hercher, discusses to close out this week.

People Inc.’s referral traffic from Google search is down 70% over the past two years, and by 26% in Q3 alone. But its digital revenue is still growing, albeit slowly.

On Tuesday, Chord, a six-year-old commerce tech startup, acquired Zenlytic, an AI startup with an anthropomorphized data analyst agent named “Zoë,” for $5 million.

If you ask the executive leadership of Affle and Perion why the two companies are merging, the answer you’ll get is “synergies.”

A combo of Tubi, sports and political ads powered Fox’s growth this last quarter, even as Fox News lost viewers and the Roku deal awaits DOJ clearance.

Starting in Q4, Reddit will test logged-in-only mode to protect its user engagement, improve ad targeting and keep AI from scraping its content.

DoorDash on Thursday confirmed the rumors and announced its intention to acquire Instacart at a $17 billion valuation.

#7609. Ignition, Inc.: MSP Mac Help Desk Guru (work from home)

Ignition is one of the oldest Apple Technical Partners on the planet, and the only fractional IT firm that specializes in the venture-backed technology ecosystem.

Fully Remote · Work from home · Full-time (Eastern or Pacific time zones) · Apple-first

ignitionit.com is a seasoned, Apple-first MSP — in business for almost 30 years — and we're hiring a Help Desk Technician to be the friendly, capable first voice our clients reach when something isn't working. This position is a remote, work-from-home, full-time role.

We've written this as a junior-to-mid-level job description because that's where most great people start on our team. But if you're more seasoned — comfortable in identity, MDM, or security work — don't scroll past. We'd be delighted to find someone who can step in higher up the ladder, and we'll happily talk about a more senior scope and comp if that's you.

Unlike many IT shops, we believe that the technology is the tactic. The actual job is making people feel taken care of. One of our core values is “49% tech support, 51% human support.”

You'll succeed by configuring devices, resetting access, untangling email, and chasing down the gremlin that's been haunting someone's conference room. But you'll know you succeeded when a client exhales and says, “Thank goodness you're on it!” That Warm Fuzzy Feeling™ is the actual product. The green lights on the dashboard are just how we get there.

Onboard a new hire at a fast-growing startup: provision their Mac, set up their Google Workspace or Microsoft 365 accounts, enroll the device in MDM, and make sure day one feels effortless.

Offboard a departing employee cleanly — recover the laptop, revoke access, and close the loop so nothing's left dangling. All boxes checked, ticket notated and closed, client followed up with.

Field a "my email stopped working" ticket that turns out to be a DNS thing, a phishing-filter thing, or a "they changed their password on their phone three weeks ago" thing.

Help a family office or RIA get a touchy Zoom Room or conference-room AV setup behaving before a meeting — over the phone.

Triage the queue so phones get answered fast, emails don't rot, and nobody feels forgotten — even when the honest answer is, “We're on it, but here's the realistic timeline."

⠀ You'll be the front line: helping with what you can, researching what you can't, and pinging the rest of the team when you're genuinely stuck. That last part is a skill, not a weakness — knowing when to ask is half the job.

We're one of the oldest Apple Technical Partners on the planet, and one of the only certified Apple Premier Partners — that’s kinda like getting knighted by the ghost of Steve Jobs. We started where you’d expect to find Macs (creative agencies, non-profits, education) but our primary clients today are cutting-edge, venture-backed AI SaaS startups, VC and private equity firms, registered investment advisors — many of them operating under stringent compliance expectations (SOC 2, SEC). That means we hold ourselves to a higher standard than the scrappy shop we started as. Polished, reliable, security-minded work is the baseline now — but always with a smile!

What hasn't changed: relationships are still our most valuable currency — with clients, with vendors, and with each other. We're a tight, supportive team. We teach each other what we know, cover for each other when life throws a punch, and care a little too much about doing things the right way. We're still a bit weird, and our clients seem to like us that way.

We move fast, priorities shift, it’s not always documented (whatever it is), our tool set and list of supported platforms is sprawling, and some days the to-do list is longer than you'd like. If you can stay warm under pressure, create order out of chaos, learn new stuff fast because you love it, and speak up when you need help, you'll thrive here.

If you need a rigid, fully-documented, never-changes environment where nobody trusts you with admin access, where you will be micro-managed so you never have to wonder whether or not you’re doing the right thing, this isn't it. You’ll have a ton of independence on our team, and freedom to use your best judgment to get the ball over the finish line, but that also means we expect you to be naturally responsible, honest, and highly accountable — to yourself, your teammates, and the clients. As they say, the price of freedom is eternal vigilance.

The tech you'll work with (and grow into)

Apple at the core — macOS, iOS, Apple Business Manager, and MDM (Jamf / Iru / Intune / Workspace ONE / and more)

Yes, PCs too — about one-third of our users are driving Windows

Google Workspace and Microsoft 365 admin consoles

Identity and access — SSO, MFA, and security keys (Okta, Entra ID, Yubikey, and friends)

Lots of other security tools — our stack is constantly evolving and may vary from client to client

The everyday productivity stack — Slack, Zoom, conference-room AV, networking basics (Meraki), and endpoint tooling

⠀ You don't need to know all of this. You need to be the kind of person who wants to. As you grow, there's a clear path into infrastructure administration, project architecture and implementation, and — for the right person — security and compliance work (phishing simulations, endpoint detection, SOC 2 / CIS / SEC readiness, due diligence questionnaire support, etc.). That's where our most senior people live, and it's wide open.

The hard requirements — we won't move forward unless you:

Can work standard business hours in Eastern or Pacific time zones (we currently need both)

Have a quiet home workspace and reliable broadband

Have proven Apple aptitude — you actually use and like the Apple ecosystem

Have at least 5 years of IT support experience on the job.

⠀ Everything else — and this is the longer list, on purpose. We figure technical skills are teachable; character takes a lot longer. So we're looking for someone who:

Genuinely cares — about clients, teammates, and doing right by people

Loves to learn, and proves it in how they spend their time

Reads, and writes clearly — clear writing is clear thinking, and you'll do a lot of it

Stays calm and kind with a frustrated person on the other end of the line

Can tell the difference between good customer service and fantastic customer service, and refuses to settle for the former

Notices when something's being done inefficiently and fixes it (you may boast about it later, that’s fine)

Proofreads their own work (yes, we noticed whether you proofread your application)

Has a sense of humor, and doesn't take themselves too seriously

Our company founder/CEO is headquartered in the Bay Area. We work with innovative, ambitious companies developing AI products. Our team members hold a range of opinions about whether AI is “good or bad” for humans, but at the end of the day, we embrace the plain fact that it is here, we must embrace it to evolve, and our clients increasingly depend on us to help them embrace it, too, to help them evolve and stay competitive.

Our CEO's opinion: AI will not replace human labor any time soon; rather, AI is a new opportunity to either (a) get things done faster, or (b) get a much higher quality of output than before. #7608. Down To The Wire To Acquire; Meta Wants To Be TV, Too

Are we in for a year-ending blockbuster M&A spree?

The Information jokes that CEOs ought to “get your deals in while ya still can, folks.”

A convergence of factors could make for a splashy Q4. As AdExchanger discussed in our Big Story Podcast last week, The Trump administration hasn’t been opposing acquisitions that would have drawn tough scrutiny under the Biden admin. Well, DoorDash CEO Tony Xu confirmed to The Information that he backed out of the company’s previous attempt to buy Instacart in 2021 because he worried Biden-era regulators would squash it.

Another factor in M&A’s favor: Many valuable businesses are struggling with risk-averse investors who don’t know how the AI revolution will shake out. The Information cites Duolingo, Coursera and Zoom as companies that have lost investor support but that would be attractive to buyers. They could join Bumble or Roku in limping to an exit.

Interestingly, what Duolingo, Coursera and Zoom have in common is that they’ve put little effort into earning ad revenue. In 2021, Zoom briefly tested a pilot ad program to monetize free users. That went away a year later.

These companies have the scaled user bases and first-party data assets marketers covet, but not much appetite for the ads biz. Could M&A flip the switch?

If YouTube’s TV, And Meta’s TV, Then Who’s Flying The Plane?

Everyone’s sick of the “Is YouTube TV?” debate. Great news: Now we can argue about whether Meta is TV, instead!

Last week, Meta announced that it’s testing long-form content on Instagram, allowing creators to share content up to 90 minutes long. The announcement comes alongside an influx of CTV spending among direct-to-consumer brands as platforms court midsize advertisers.

Cody Plofker, former CEO and CMO of makeup brand Jones Road, had been against TV advertising until he realized spending 80% of the company budget on Meta was limiting brand exposure, he said at Tatari’s Forward event in New York on Thursday.

Like Jones Road, many DTC brands have “[maxed] out social platforms” and are now putting more focus on TV advertising “as a performance vehicle,” Mike Shields writes in Next in Media.

And CTV ad platforms like Tatari are taking inspiration from Meta and Google by launching their own optimization engines.

Never one to back down from a fight, Meta is searching for its own spot in the TV landscape.

But YouTube is already known for engaged, loyal followings, Shields points out. And YouTube’s content is delivered on demand, which is a fit for TV, whereas Instagram’s algorithmic feed isn’t the traditional TV experience.

As one insider in the creator market tells Shields, why take away what’s working on YouTube TV and redirect resources to Instagram TV?

AI search is the new boogeyman robbing publishers of ad revenue. But another long-feared boogeyman – brand safety – can still spook the sell side.

Last week, former writers for the feminist news site Jezebel raised the alarm that hundreds of articles had been removed from the site. They pointed the finger at Jezebel’s new owner, Paste Magazine, which acquired the publication from G/O Media in 2023.

Anna Merlan, a former Jezebel writer now reporting for Mother Jones, says she heard from sources familiar with Paste that its publisher, William Sagan, decided to remove the articles after an “advertising and analytics company” flagged more than 4,000 articles as “not brand safe.”

But Sagan denied that Paste deleted the articles over brand safety concerns in statements provided to Mother Jones and The Washington Post. He says Paste often flags articles for any number of reasons, including grammatical errors, and temporarily reverts these stories to “draft” status. Indeed, many of the Jezebel articles taken down last week were republished soon after their authors started raising questions.

Paste’s exact motivation for taking the articles down remains unclear. But you can’t blame former Jezebel writers for being sensitive about brand safety.

Jezebel has long suffered monetization troubles tied to advertiser concerns over its coverage. Former Paste editor-in-chief Josh Jackson even claimed he never knew the extent to which brand safety solutions can demonetize publisher content until Paste acquired Jezebel.

Challenger social platforms saw their stock prices drop significantly after reporting Q3 earnings on Thursday. Reddit shares fell 29% and Roblox dropped 17% on Friday due to user growth concerns, while Pinterest dipped 3% after missing ad revenue expectations. [Yahoo Finance]

#7607. Court seems poised to side with Catholic preschools in religious discrimination dispute

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

The Supreme Court on Tuesday appeared ready to hold that the exclusion of Catholic preschools in Colorado from the state’s universal preschool program violates the First Amendment. After just over two hours of oral argument in St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy, a majority seemed to agree with the challengers that Colorado’s refusal to provide them with an exemption from rules that would require the preschools to admit all students – including LGBTQ children and children with LGBTQ parents – should be subject to a more stringent constitutional test than that applied by the lower court. The court could decide to apply that standard itself or send the case back to the lower courts for them to do so.

Colorado launched the universal preschool program, which provides families in the state with up to 15 hours of free preschool per week at participating schools, in 2023. To participate in the program, preschools must meet a variety of state standards and sign a nondiscrimination agreement, in which they consent to “provide eligible children an equal opportunity to enroll and receive preschool services regardless of race, ethnicity, religious affiliation, sexual orientation, gender identity, lack of housing, income level, or disability.” The preschools cannot decline to serve LGBTQ families, because Colorado believes such refusals would violate the nondiscrimination agreement.

The plaintiffs – the Archdiocese of Denver, two Catholic parishes with preschools (one of which has since closed), and two parents of preschool-aged children – went to federal court to challenge the state’s policy. They contended that requiring Catholic preschools to agree to the nondiscrimination agreement to participate in the universal preschool program constitutes unlawful religious discrimination and that the First Amendment requires Colorado to carve out a religious exemption that allows them to take part in the program.

After both the district court and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 10th Circuit rejected the challengers’ claim, they came to the Supreme Court last year, asking the justices to take up the case – which the court agreed in April 2026 to do.

Representing the challengers, Nicholas Reaves told the justices that the schools in the Archdiocese of Denver “exist to pass on the faith to the next generation.” “[T]his is not a zero-sum game,” he said, because “letting Catholic schools” participate in the universal preschool program “will create more seats for everyone.”

Representing the state, Colorado Deputy Solicitor General Helen Norton countered that “Colorado welcomes religious preschools to” the program and allows them to teach their religious beliefs. It simply asks them, she emphasized, to comply with the same rules as everyone else.

One of the major points of contention at Tuesday’s argument was the significance of the Supreme Court’s 2022 decision in Carson v. Makin, in which the court struck down a Maine law that allowed public funding to be used for private schools, but not for schools that provide religious instruction. The case was the third in a trilogy of decisions on the availability of public funding for religious institutions. In Carson, the majority applied strict scrutiny – the toughest constitutional test – after it concluded that the Maine law barred some private schools from receiving public funds “solely because they are religious.”

In response to a question from Justice Clarence Thomas about whether a ruling for the challengers would require the court to extend its ruling in Carson, Reaves responded that it would not. In Carson, he insisted, the court’s “focus … was to look at … what is happening to the religious believer?” The court in Carson, he said, “didn’t focus on the text of the law in Maine. It focused on whether schools are being excluded on account of their religious exercise.”

Chief Justice John Roberts pressed Reaves on that point, observing that the law at issue in Carson specifically discriminated against religious schools – which, Roberts suggested, is not the case with the Colorado program.

Reaves pushed back. He noted that the laws in other cases involving public benefits had been neutral, rather than discriminating against religious people or organizations – for example, the court’s 1963 decision in Sherbert v. Verner, reversing a ruling by the South Carolina Supreme Court that had rejected a constitutional challenge to the denial of employment benefits from a Seventh-day Adventist whose religion barred her from working on Saturday.

Roberts later questioned Norton on a related point, asking her to differentiate the Colorado program from the law at issue in Carson and telling her that the effect of the Maine law was “pretty much the same as the effect of the law here.” He also told Norton that the state was trying to “bury Sherbert” even though “nothing in our precedent has backed away from” it.

Two of the court’s Democratic appointees, however, echoed Roberts’ initial skepticism that Carson dictated the outcome of the challengers’ case. Justice Elena Kagan told Reaves that the trilogy of cases culminating in Carson involved laws that had excluded religious institutions and schools because of their religion. “[I]t was a nondiscrimination principle,” she emphasized, but “you’re asking us to” issue a decision that would go “far beyond” its earlier cases. In particular, she suggested, the challengers were seeking a ruling that religious people “need a special accommodation” because of their faith.

Reaves responded that an interpretation of the court’s decision in Carson that focused on whether the law at issue expressly discriminated against religion would be “very easy to circumvent.”

Kagan responded that this isn’t “a good case to raise the kind of specter of circumvention.” “[T]his is a case,” she continued, “of a state trying to enforce its own nondiscrimination principles.”

Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson appeared to agree. She characterized Carson as a case that prohibited governments from treating religious schools worse than it treated secular schools. That doctrine, she posited, was “pretty narrow” and made “perfect sense.” But, she told Reaves, “your schools want to discriminate by exclusion” when no other school participating in the universal preschool program does so.

Some of the court’s Republican appointees were more persuaded by the challengers’ argument – also advanced by Sarah Harris, the principal deputy solicitor general who argued on behalf of the Trump administration in support of the challengers – that Carson should apply even if the Colorado law does not specifically target religion.

Justice Neil Gorsuch, for example, asked “what would be left” of cases like Sherbert “if everything turned on express discrimination” against religion, while Justice Samuel Alito appeared dubious that the legislators who enacted the Colorado universal preschool law “would not understand what the effect of” the law’s requirements “would be.”

Similarly, Justice Amy Coney Barrett asked Norton why, if Colorado cannot expressly exclude religious schools from its program, it can “impose a condition” – the nondiscrimination requirement – that it knows “schools will be unable to agree to?” Barrett pointed to a New York Times op-ed written in the wake of Carson by law professor Aaron Tang, who she stated suggested that states counteract some of the effects of Carson by enacting nondiscrimination requirements.

Norton resisted any effort to link Colorado’s nondiscrimination requirement to an intent to target religious schools, stressing that there was no evidence of the legislature’s motives and (in response to a question from Jackson) that the requirement predated the inclusion of religious schools in the program.

The justices and advocates also debated, although less extensively than the significance of Carson, whether Colorado’s conditions were neutral and generally applied to every preschool, regardless of religion – the kind of government actions, the Supreme Court held in 1990 in Employment Division v. Smith, that are subject to a less stringent constitutional test, known as rational-basis review.

Reaves told the justices that the Colorado nondiscrimination requirement was not the kind of “across-the-board” prohibition that the court envisioned in Smith because the Colorado law contains a series of preferences to facilitate the matching of families to preschools, including a “catch-all” preference that allows preschools to request (and the state to grant) a preference not listed in the regulation. Moreover, he added, the law also creates exceptions to accommodate children with disabilities and children from low-income families.

For her part, Norton characterized the preferences as very different from the kind of exclusion that the challengers seek. Even if a school receives a preference, she stressed, it is still subject to the nondiscrimination requirement.

Justice Brett Kavanaugh appeared to approach the case from what he regarded as a practical angle, asking Norton why the state wouldn’t “seek the win/win?” With over 2,000 preschools participating in the Colorado program, he said, there should be “plenty of opportunities to respect the rights of the religious believers” and, at the same time, “the ability of LGBT parents” to find a school that is a good fit for their families. “Why,” he asked, “has this been provoked?”

Justice Sonia Sotomayor took a different tack, suggesting that a ruling for the challengers could have broader implications. A Catholic preschool, she told Reaves, could reject a child “merely” because his or her parents are LGBTQ. Would this, she queried, also allow a religious preschool to turn down Black children?

Reaves said that it would not. He pointed to a 1983 case in which the Supreme Court, applying strict scrutiny, upheld the Internal Revenue Service’s decision to revoke the tax-exempt status of a private university and private school with racially discriminatory admissions policies. The government in that case, he emphasized, indicated that its interest in prohibiting such policies was not merely “compelling” (the first factor under strict scrutiny) but “overriding.”

He told the justices that strict scrutiny should similarly apply to this case. “And then the government can come forward and say we have a really good reason for” excluding Catholic preschools from the program. But, he concluded, “we just don’t think they’ve done that in this case.”

By the end of the argument, Sotomayor seemed to leave little doubt about where she stood. “No matter what line of cases we follow,” she said, “there will be tremendous problems and a great cost to someone.”

A decision is expected sometime next year.

Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

The finale of Chicken Shop Date will be screened in movie theaters. Amelia Dimoldenberg is ending her iconic interview series, but Chicken Shop Date is going out with a bang. Caylus is entering the consumer goods market by popping his own popcorn. Bluesky is letting creators link to the platforms they use to generate revenue. The high court ruled that regulators have the right to enforce the Online Safety Act, which requires platforms to provide a safe experience for younger users.

A hijacked QR code turned Lacy’s on-stream dinner into a nightmare. The Twitch star says that he ran up an unintended bill of approximately $12,000 after his viewers manipulated a QR code they noticed at the Japanese restaurant where he was eating. Note to streamers: Maybe blur out QR codes when you go out to eat, or, if it’s easier, just get nicer fans.

#7598. AI Labels Don’t Tell Consumers Whether An Ad’s Claims Are Real

Disclosure: Sourin Chakrabarti works on AI labeling for advertising at Meta. The views expressed are his own and do not represent Meta.

In October 2025, three clips appearing to show police detaining and pepper-spraying protesters racked up millions of views across X, Instagram and TikTok. Created with OpenAI’s Sora, the videos carried visible watermarks, yet NewsGuard found that users still cited them as evidence that the events occurred. The footage crossed an unsettling threshold: It didn’t just look realistic; it functioned as visual proof.

Most concern about deepfakes has focused on politics. But the same tactic is now appearing in advertising, where synthetic content can make a product claim look proven.

In a recent campaign investigated by Full Fact, a supposed doctor claiming to be affiliated with Guy’s and St Thomas’ NHS Foundation Trust tested a weight-loss patch and appeared to grow thinner on camera. The trust called the posts “completely fraudulent,” while Google’s Gemini detected SynthID watermarks confirming AI involvement. Yet that watermark only revealed that AI was involved, not where the fiction ended. Was only the doctor’s face synthetic? Or were the medical authority, hospital connection, personal experience and physical transformation invented, too?

This exposes the fundamental blind spot of AI disclosures: they flag the production tool, not the illusion. A generic label tells consumers that AI was used to build an ad, but leaves them to guess where reality ends and fiction begins.

The fraudulent NHS weight-loss ad was not an isolated incident. In 2025, the Australian Medical Association warned that deepfakes impersonating prominent doctors were promoting unproven products, with clinicians discovering the fraud only when patients asked whether to swap prescribed treatments for advertised miracle cures. In 2026, Chinese regulators launched an enforcement campaign targeting businesses that mass-produced fabricated consumer-experience posts.

The legal principle predates generative AI. In FTC v. Colgate-Palmolive Co., a shaving cream commercial used a plexiglass prop in place of real sandpaper. Viewers were misled because the simulation was presented as a genuine product test. The case offers a useful test for AI advertising today: Does an ad merely illustrate a claim or does it ask viewers to treat a synthetic scene as real-world proof?

Platforms and regulators are building substantial disclosure systems to track synthetic content. Google displays “How this ad was made” panels, Meta attaches “AI info” labels and TikTok offers “AIGC” self-disclosure controls. Governments are pushing in the same direction: The European Union’s Article 50 rules require transparency for synthetic media, China mandates explicit AI markers and New York requires advertisements to identify synthetic performers.

Yet current AI-labeling systems mostly tell consumers that AI was used, not what it changed or why it matters. The same label can appear on an ad with a decorative AI background and one with an entirely fabricated testimonial. Those uses are not equally misleading, but a generic label may not distinguish between them.

Some policies address the clearest cases. The Advertising Standards Council of India’s 2026 draft guidance identifies fabricated experts, endorsements and exaggerated results as high-risk uses that labeling alone cannot fix. TikTok Shop prohibits AI-generated professional identities used to sell health products and alterations that misrepresent product performance. But a harder question remains: What about AI simulations that are lawful but could still be mistaken for real-world evidence?

The disclosure gap is becoming urgent as AI ad generation reaches industrial scale. In 2025, advertisers created three times as many Gemini-generated assets on Google as in 2024, including nearly 70 million in the final quarter alone. Meta has reportedly aimed to automate ad creation and targeting with AI by the end of 2026. Because these tools are embedded directly into ad-creation systems, safeguards cannot rely on post hoc consumer complaints. They must operate systematically across millions of ads.

The answer is not to label every synthetic pixel. Building on the IAB’s January 2026 disclosure framework, regulators should adopt a risk-based approach requiring specific disclosures whenever AI material appears to provide evidence for a product claim. This approach would produce three outcomes:

Platforms could implement this approach by requiring advertisers to disclose three things: the role played by any AI-created person or scene, whether the generated material depicts product performance or results and what real-world evidence supports the claim. Meta, Google and TikTok already accept advertiser declarations, so these questions could fit into existing workflows. Platforms should also retain a record of the advertiser’s answers and the notice shown to consumers, creating an auditable trail of how each ad was reviewed and presented. An emerging industry proposal calls this a served disclosure receipt.

Consider the weight-loss patch video. Under this system, an “AI was used” label would be only the starting point. The advertiser would have to identify the doctor as a synthetic expert, classify the apparent transformation as a product-performance claim and clarify whether the testimonial represented a real customer. It would also have to provide evidence supporting the weight-loss claim. If the doctor was falsely presented as real, the testimonial was fabricated or the result lacked substantiation, the ad would not be approved.

The goal is labels that answer the question consumers actually face: not just whether AI made the ad but whether AI made up the reason to buy.

“Data-Driven Thinking” is written by members of the media community and contains fresh ideas on the digital revolution in media.

#7595. Fox Doesn’t Want To Talk About Roku, But It’s Got Lots To Say About Tubi And Politics

Any investor hoping to ask about Fox’s pending Roku acquisition during its fiscal Q1 2027 earnings call on Monday was out of luck.

Fox’s IR rep made that clear up front and pointed analysts to Fox’s SEC filings instead.

However, CEO Lachlan Murdoch did share a mini update, including that shareholder and foreign regulatory approvals are in, although Fox is still working with the DOJ on antitrust clearance.

“[We] expect to close the transaction as soon as we can,” Murdoch told investors, noting that Fox’s “conviction in the opportunity has only grown.” Pairing Roku’s platform with Fox’s sports, news and entertainment content is a good recipe for building “our position in the fastest-growing segments of the media landscape,” he said.

Fox’s revenue rose 22% to $4.6 billion in the quarter, including a 47% jump in advertising revenue (60% in its TV segment) driven by the World Cup, early midterm spending and Tubi, its free ad-supported streaming service.

Tubi grew revenue 35% year over year, alongside a 23% uptick in total view time.

Fox attributed that engagement to a combo of Tubi’s content library, 10 new originals and a World Cup hub, which drew on Fox’s US English-language rights to the tournament.

Tubi also got a boost from viral content from more than 600 creators. Its Tubi for Creators program launched in 2025 with six creators and has since wooed big YouTube names like MrBeast and Jomboy Media.

And profits are growing, too, despite higher content costs, according to CFO Steve Tomsic, who noted that Tubi is contributing more to the bottom line than it was in the year-ago quarter when it turned its first profit – a development Murdoch himself apparently didn’t see coming.

A Bank of America analyst on the call reminded Murdoch that a year or so ago he’d said that Tubi’s growth, then in the midteens, wouldn’t be sustainable.

“I don’t remember saying that, but I’m sure I did … Thank you for calling me out on that one,” Murdoch said, adding that Tubi’s profit margins should settle in the 20% range once it reaches “further maturity.”

Advertising is the main engine behind Tubi’s momentum, which Murdoch said is continuing into the current quarter. Tubi’s audience is young, diverse and mostly cord-free, he said, which is like catnip for advertisers.

“They’re a very hard market for advertisers to reach,” he said, which, in a midterm year, is a pretty good pitch to political campaigns.

Fox booked more than $350 million in political ads this cycle, and Tubi was responsible for roughly $50 million of that.

Most of the rest – $250 million-plus – went to Fox’s local stations, including many in battleground states, where demand is so high that some stations run out of ad inventory. The remaining $50-ish million went to political ads across national sports, news and entertainment.

But if you squint, and not that hard, Tubi also kind of counts as local advertising in Murdoch’s view. “It’s effectively local revenue because it’s targeted,” he said.

Politics aside, sports has been a tailwind, too.

The FIFA World Cup final was the most-watched soccer telecast in US history; the World Series, which aired on Fox, averaged 12 million viewers; and Fox’s NFL “America’s Game of the Week” is drawing an average of nearly 25 million viewers per game.

But Murdoch was also careful to temper expectations for Fox One, Fox’s streaming service for Fox content.

It’s not like there’s a World Cup every year – or a midterm election.

“It’s always a point in time,” Murdoch said. “Every couple years, you’ve got to be careful to understand the strength of the political cycle.”

And not everything at Fox was a win this past quarter, no matter how you spin it.

Fox News finished its fiscal Q1 as the most-watched cable news network, with 2.1 million primetime viewers and 1.3 million across all dayparts. But those figures were down 17% and 16% year over year, according to Nielsen, and Fox News was the only major cable news network to see declines. The slide has continued into October, when total-day ratings fell 27% ahead of the midterms.

Murdoch blamed tough comps against last year’s “tremendous news cycle,” which included the inauguration, Charlie Kirk’s assassination and DOGE-related drama. He compared this cycle to the 2006 midterms, when a second-term president was halfway through his term.

It’s not that viewers are defecting to CNN or MS Now, he said. They’re “just fatigued and watching slightly less television overall.” (Even so, Nielsen does show CNN and MS Now both up from last year.)

Meanwhile, cable advertising rose 8%, helped along by sports, but digital news ad revenue fell. Asked about that – we mourn you preemptively, open web – Murdoch pointed to Fox News Digital’s standing as the top news site in the US and called digital news a “hyper-competitive market.”

#7593. A new California law lets children of family vloggers make their parents take down all footage of them

A new California law will protect the children of family vloggers once they turn 18.

Senate Bill No. 1247 gives adults whose parents, legal guardians, or family members used them in social media content while they were minors the right to demand removal of said content.

Once served a notice of removal, parents/guardians/etc have 10 days to take down violative content or edit it to remove the requester’s appearances. If those 10 days pass and the content is still up, vloggers will face penalties of $3,000 per day moving forward, plus further potential damages, injunctive relief, and attorney’s fees.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

Now, to be clear, this law won’t let someone take their mom to court for posting Facebook pictures of them in an embarrassing Halloween costume (though we do think parents should more carefully consider what they post about their kid online, especially in the age of AI).

S.B. 1247 has a couple requirements that tune it to specifically target professional family vloggers.

We’re guessing it could potentially apply if a parent signed a financial agreement with a family vlogger to have their kid appear in the family’s content on a regular basis, but that circumstance isn’t accounted for in S.B. 1247’s current form.

The law will also lay a mandate on social media platforms: Once it kicks in, YouTube, TikTok, Instagram, and all other sites “shall provide a clear and conspicuous mechanism by which a child influencer can request a vlogger” remove content featuring them, according to the bill’s text. If a platform doesn’t have a built-in mechanism, it has to be responsible for receiving removal requests, and is required to forward those requests to vloggers within three days of receipt.

Vloggers who receive removal requests and comply with them will not face any consequences. It’s only if they refuse removal or if removal takes longer than 10 days that they open themselves up to further legal action.

This law kicks in in January 2027–and while it’s only a California law, we do expect other states might enact similar protections. YouTube just turned 20 years old, so the vlogging industry has now been around long enough that thousands of kids whose parents once featured them in videos are turning 18 and gaining control over their own lives. S.B. 1247 makes sure that control is retroactive, too.

The mini K-drama follows two classmates whose destinies intertwine during late-night runs to (of course) the local 7-Eleven. A short trailer captures a 7-Eleven employee/classic Korean uncle telling the two not-so-star-crossed lovers that they should notice: opposites attract.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

And some of the most memorable ones happen over something as simple as a late-night meal at a convenience store,” Danny Lee, A Convenient Love‘s director, said in a statement. “That’s what made 7-Eleven’s new Korean-inspired menu a natural fit. We built 7 vertical episodes around it and shot all of them in a real 7-Eleven with the food at every turning point. Pizza aside, the Flavors of Korea collection includes a gochujang remix on 7-Eleven’s iconic egg salad sando, gochujang boneless wings, bibigo spicy chicken dumplings, a KBBQ taquito, a KBBQ hot dog, and somyeon with kimchi.

Combining the two could push A Convenient Love to a level other branded series have yet to reach. We’re curious to see how it pays off.
